title: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline
body_text: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Home News US & Canada UK UK Politics England N. Ireland N. Ireland Politics Scotland Scotland Politics Wales Wales Politics Africa Asia China India Australia Europe Latin America Middle East In Pictures BBC InDepth BBC Verify Sport Business World of Business Technology of Business NYSE Opening Bell Technology Watch Documentaries Artificial Intelligence Intelligence Revolution AI v the Mind Tech Now Health Watch Documentaries Culture Watch Documentaries Film & TV Music Art & Design Style Books Entertainment News Arts Watch Documentaries Arts in Motion Travel Watch Documentaries Destinations Africa Antarctica Asia Australia and Pacific Caribbean & Bermuda Central America Europe Middle East North America South America World’s Table Culture & Experiences Adventures The SpeciaList To the Ends of the Earth Earth Watch Documentaries Science Natural Wonders Climate Solutions Sustainable Business Green Living Audio Podcast Categories Radio Audio FAQs Video Watch Documentaries BBC Maestro Discover the World Live Live News Live Sport Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Becca Warner BBC/Serenity Strull (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Birdwatching can help slow brain ageing and is increasingly being used as therapy for dementia patients. Every week, a group of elderly birders spend hours hunkering down inside a wooden hide in the English countryside, peering through binoculars as they excitedly share what they spot. An oystercatcher's long, bright beak probing the pebbled ground; two great crested grebes bobbing in the water, their plumed heads poised. Most of these birdwatchers have difficulty recalling what happened earlier that day, and might struggle to follow a conversation. But they become animated when swapping notes on the birds that fill the sky around Forge Mill Lake in the UK's West Midlands. Among them is 78-year-old Harold*. He loved the outdoors when he was younger, but more recently dementia has made him withdrawn and anxious. His daughter Lucy* brought him here, hoping that the change of scenery and peaceful lake might be good for him. After an apprehensive start, Harold began smiling when someone pointed out a robin and enjoyed watching the ducks splashing in the water. Blue tits darted between the nearby trees, and Lucy saw Harold laugh for the first time in a long time. "For that moment in time he was present in the moment, he wasn't worried about his memory or his confidence. That is very powerful, in a gentle way," says Jenny Budinger, a community dementia advisor at Age UK, the non-profit that runs the birdwatching group. Birdwatching is increasingly recognised as a valuable way for elderly people and dementia patients to spend their time, with groups set up in nursing homes in the UK, Germany and the US. Paying attention to birds , even through the window, can help older people feel more connected to others, experience more positive emotions and boost memory skills. Now new research shows that birdwatching can reshape the brain, much like learning an athletic sport or a musical instrument – and may even help slow the brain's ageing. Better-organised brains In the laboratory, neuroscientists tested keen birdwatchers' identification skills to determine who was an expert and who was a novice, then looked at their brains. The scientists found that the very structure of experts' brains was different – and that birdwatching expertise might slow age-related decline by keeping the brain more organised. Erik Wing, who led this research at Baycrest Academy for Research and Education in Toronto, Canada, compared MRI brain scans from bird experts to those of novices while they identified birds. He found that expert brains were wired differently in regions important for functions like attention, visual perception and visual recognition. Among expert birders, these regions showed more activity – particularly when they were asked to identify birds they weren't already familiar with. The findings don't prove whether structural brain differences are the cause or effect of birdwatching expertise. But, Wing says, one explanation is that the areas of the brain used for birdwatching might undergo "neuroplasticity" – the ability to change shape and function over time. BBC/Serenity Strull Birdwatching can reshape the brain and may help slow ageing (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) Wing also analysed how organised the birdwatchers' brains were. Organisation in the brain tends to reduce with age, and lower measures of organisation are associated with reduced cognition . In experts' brains, some regions had higher levels of organisation and coherence than novices of the same age. Some of these regions were also the ones that showed more activity during bird identification. This indicates a "kind of preservation of organisation" in the brains of experts as they age, Wing says. More research is needed to understand the nature of this preservation and how it links to wider cognitive function. But for now, the results may indicate that "acquiring this skill earlier in life might produce benefits that continue through to older adults", Wing says. This is good news for the many Gen Z (16 to 29-year-old) birdwatchers who are getting their binoculars out long before old age sets in. Bird therapy Wing's research looked at birdwatching expertise, but other findings suggest that there may be psychological benefits to birdwatching even for those without special knowledge or skills. In fact, when it comes to experiencing psychological restoration – feelings of calm, freedom and rejuvenation – enthusiasm may be more relevant than expertise . A study of 388 birdwatchers in Poland found that those who say they are more interested in birding than other activities and consider it an important part of their lives are more likely to experience psychological restoration than birdwatchers who are highly skilled but less enthusiastic. Simply choosing to be interested in birds, then, could have its own benefits. Elisabeth Kals, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the Catholic University of Eichstätt-Ingolstadt in Germany, is interested in how our relationship with nature shapes our life experiences and wellbeing. She studied what happened when people living in nursing homes had the chance to watch the local bird life. Her team installed bird feeding stations outside 65 homes, positioned so that residents could watch the birds from the comfort of the indoor common area, and assessed the residents' cognition, mobility and wellbeing through self-reports and inputs from staff and family. They saw improvements after just a few weeks, and after a month birdwatching explained residents' wellbeing better than their age and care level. "The findings were clearly positive," Kals says. Those who took part in birdwatching became more cognitively agile, she adds – meaning they were more able to follow a conversation and interact with family who visited, remember and recognise birds that had visited before, and show alertness. Nursing home staff were the first to see the difference the birds made. "For weeks, they haven't seen a smile on [a resident's] face, and then they see the smile," Kals says. Some of the memory and concentration improvements are evident after just three to four weeks, Kals says. Her team's findings have prompted German health insurance companies – who, among others, initially funded the research project – to invest in setting up bird feeders and viewing areas in more than 400 nursing homes across Bavaria. "It was so effective, it just economised money," Kals says. BBC/Serenity Strull Even paying attention to birds through a window can have a positive influence (Credit: BBC/Serenity Strull) In the US, a similar initiative was set up at four care communities in 2013 in Connecticut, and later in Texas and Colorado . Bird Tales is a therapy programme for people living with dementia that involves installing bird feeders in the facilities where they live and giving them stuffed bird animals that make bird-like calls so they can learn about different species. The result has been positive for those taking part: they report finding it cognitively stimulating and say it connects them with the past. A similar programme has seen benefits for survivors of stroke, some of whom experience aphasia – difficulty speaking or understanding spoken language. The University of Montana's Intensive Comprehensive Aphasia Program started with owl spotting in 2021, and now includes guided observations and call identification of Montana's diverse bird population. Why does watching birds have such a positive impact on how we feel and think? For Kals, it's "not just about birds as such; it is about nature, attention, emotion, meaning, social exchange, and activity coming together in a very simple way. It creates small moments of curiosity – pleasure, anticipation". And, she adds, it is "extremely accessible". This may be why, in a UK survey of dementia patients and their carers, watching birds and other wildlife was the second most popular outdoor activity after simply walking in nature. The same survey found that challenges with transport and access are big considerations for people with dementia – which may not be such a barrier for those who can see birds from their kitchen window. Wing says birdwatching is a means of exploring curiosity, and it is perhaps this curiosity that is so beneficial. "I think there's a lot of benefit to incorporating more novelty in our lives, in midlife and as we continue to age," Wing says. Curiosity plays an important role in maintaining cognitive function later in life, possibly because it activates norepinephrine and dopamine in the brain, which have a positive, anti-inflammatory effect. For Kals, getting to know the birds that call and swoop around us is a way to remember who we are. "We are part of nature as human beings, but we lose that connection, unfortunately, quite early in life. [Birdwatching] is a way to reestablish this connection, and it's so simple." * Names have been changed for privacy reasons. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses. Pure Rust. Runs locally. Files never leave your machine. Try it in your browser → · Download · Roadmap PaperPilot is a PDF and document toolkit written in Rust. The same engine runs as: Surface Use it for MCP server Give Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, Pi, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP client the ability to merge, split, OCR, and compress PDFs CLI Batch and scripted workflows Browser (WASM) Zero-install tools; files are processed in browser memory, nothing is uploaded Desktop app Tauri + Svelte GUI with viewer, markup, and diff Local REST API Call it from Python, Node, or n8n at localhost:7823 No Chromium, no C++ runtime, no cloud calls. Quick start 1. Use it with your coding agent (MCP) Codex, Claude Code, Kimi Code, and current Pi releases connect to the same local stdio server. See the coding agent setup guide for each client's configuration and verification steps. Builds from this source can also print ready-to-merge configuration: paperpilot-mcp --client-config codex # Also: claude-code, kimi-code, pi, claude-desktop, cursor Download paperpilot-mcp from Releases , then add it to claude_desktop_config.json : { "mcpServers" : { "paperpilot" : { "command" : " /path/to/paperpilot-mcp " } } } Restart Claude and try: "Merge these two PDFs and compress the result." 2. Use the CLI # Merge paperpilot merge --inputs doc1.pdf doc2.pdf --output merged.pdf # Compress paperpilot compress --input in.pdf --quality 75 --output compressed.pdf # Rotate pages 1, 3–5 by 90° paperpilot rotate --input in.pdf --pages 1,3-5 --angle 90 --output out.pdf 3. Use it in the browser Go to usepaperpilot.com . Open your browser's Network tab while you work — you'll see no file uploads. 4. Build from source git clone https://github.com/KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot.git cd PaperPilot cargo build --release -p paperpilot-cli -p paperpilot-mcp -p paperpilot-gateway Desktop app: cd apps/desktop && pnpm install && pnpm tauri dev Requires Rust 1.75+, Node.js, and pnpm. What it can do today (v0.6) Organize: merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages, extract pages, booklet imposition, N-up grid Optimize: compress Extract: plain text, OCR (pure-Rust PaddleOCR via rten ) Security: watermark, validate signatures, remove signatures, PII scan, deep sanitize Office data: Excel → JSON, Excel → CSV Coming next (see ROADMAP.md ): v0.7: PDF ↔ Markdown / HTML / JSON v0.8: PDF → Word / Excel / PowerPoint v0.9: encrypt, decrypt, sign, redact, forms, annotations v1.0: render, flatten, repair, compare, PDF/A, Bates numbering Why another PDF tool? Private by default. Everything runs locally or in your browser tab. Agent-ready. MCP support is first-class, not an afterthought. One engine, many surfaces. CLI, MCP, REST, WASM, and desktop share the same Rust core, so behavior is consistent. Small and dependency-light. Pure Rust, built on lopdf , pdf_oxide , rten , and friends. Benchmarks Run cargo bench --workspace to reproduce. Methodology and results: SYSTEM_BENCHMARK_REPORT.md . Architecture Desktop (Tauri) · CLI · REST (Axum) · MCP (stdio) · WASM (browser / edge) │ Rust core workspace paperpilot-core · paperpilot-pdf · paperpilot-nlp · paperpilot-gateway paperpilot-mcp · paperpilot-wasm · paperpilot-storage Embed in your own site < script src =" https://cdn.usepaperpilot.com/embed.js " data-tools =" merge,compress,ocr " > </ script > < div id =" paperpilot-widget " > </ div > Local REST API paperpilot serve --port 7823 curl -X POST http://localhost:7823/api/v1/pdf/merge \ -H " Content-Type: application/json " \ -d ' {"inputs": ["a.pdf", "b.pdf"], "output": "out.pdf"} ' Swagger docs at http://localhost:7823/docs . Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome. Good first contributions: bug reports with a sample PDF, new tool requests, and docs fixes. License Community Edition (this repo): Apache 2.0 . It includes the CLI, MCP server, REST gateway, WASM engine, and desktop app. An Enterprise Edition (SSO, RBAC, audit logs, DLP) is developed separately. title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
body_text: “We should be more ambitious with the software we build” “We should be more ambitious with the software we build” | Patreon Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust ) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying [W]e should be more ambitious 1 with the software we build There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail , this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath , this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail , multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader 2 , this money overflow bug , etc. This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free 3 , but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed. That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post). As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday , and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever. But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold . You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use. If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more. Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were: Ripgrep Compiling Rust Syscall and filesystem overhead At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about , this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations or building a custom OS or a funny layer that fakes out syscalls would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now. For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work 0 , but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up. My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now 4 . Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls . When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena . Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed. When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher) 5 . For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh . I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats 6 . BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle 7 . I'm more productive and can work faster , but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing 8 . All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build. Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, Max Hawkins, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion. I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done. I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that would be a super interesting thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago. Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course): If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think I have a similar thought about " there's no reason for software to be slow " BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase . There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law . But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do. And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly close to a correct set of rules (approximately as close as what someone else did with much more human effort and less of a systematic approach), which was enough to compare it to someone else's implementation and get a working set of rules. This setup did cost a lot more in tokens than a more manual approach. But it was "only" a month or two of the $200/mo OpenAI subscription with GPT-5.1/5.2, which is a lower cost than the cost in time of me sitting down and writing a clean spec for the game, i.e., a copy of the rules that is actually consistent and correct. I feel like a lot of problems are in something like this class of problem, where it's possible to set up some kind of at least partially self-checking setup that a human can spend a small amount of time on. This also feels analogous to the situation about software testing at large, where (before coding agents) I found fuzzing and property-based testing to be highly effective. For most domains, people told me some kind of reason this kind of testing wouldn't work, but when I've tried these techniques with all of the domains people told me these techniques don't work for, they work fine. They're somewhat more work to apply, but they're still applicable and, AFAICT, more efficient and effective than writing traditional unit tests. Part of the gist of Yossi's comment is that people aren't doing this kind of thing. Considering how many more bugs I see now than I used to, e.g., the last time I opened up the web chat for a big AI lab, I ran into a double-digit number of bugs within one minute, it's hard to say that Yossi is wrong. But, to that point, I still have my original opinion. Just because other people are pumping out vast quantities of barely working slop doesn't mean that you have to do the same thing. Appendix: a few "random" examples The examples in the body of the post I gave for things I've done are tooling things I never would've done. There are a lot more things like that as well since it's so easy to build "works for me" quality tooling that's intended solely for me. I do think it's possible to go further than is productive, e.g., Steve Yegge wrote a lot about Gas Town and how productive it was, but when he was building his next agentic framework, he noted that he never used Gas Town to successfully build anything other than Gas Town and here's someone playing his game that's been created with his next gen framework (the commenter's references to $1B are because Yegge says his game is in the running for being the first solo-run billion dollar company), people were into Ralph Loops for a while even though, when I tried comparing them, they seemed worse than just doing the naive thing I was doing at the time, normal loops with context where you sometimes clear context as appropriate instead of doing it by default at the completely arbitrary point of when a single turn is completed , etc., so I've tried to stick to things where the impact is pretty direct. Besides the obvious reason this has been effective, the dramatic change in model and harness capability over time means that what tooling it makes sense to build changes very quickly, so spending a lot of time working on any particular tool that will be suboptimal at best and quite possibly obsolete in three months doesn't really make sense. And, for a lot of my personal tools, my assumption is that an AI lab will obsolete anything I make in short order. For a very silly example of this, I have a tool that was useful since the release of GPT-5.6 Sol that restarts codex when it finds a memory leak. Presumably, OpenAI will fix this at some point and this tool will become worthless. For a slightly less silly example, take the Rust interpreter I had some agent build. For token-budget reasons, a lot of things that ought to be done for a very high-performance interpreter haven't been done. For example, the interpreter doesn't modify the actual Rust front-end compiler to make it easy to take updates; performance would be much better if I just made changes to the Rust front-end, but I don't have the token budget to maintain a compatible fork of the Rust compiler, but this shouldn't be a problem for OpenAI. OpenAI committed $10B+ on getting access to Cerebras while also preventing Anthropic from having access. Funnily enough, for coding, on many tasks, if you actually use one of their SOTA models and compare it to what you get from Anthropic, the actual speedup isn't all that large because of time spent on things like compiling Rust. Given that they were willing to commit $10B+ on this, it stands to reason that they'll eventually do a better job at speeding up the relevant tools than anyone could feasibly do outside an AI lab, so there's not much point in spending too much effort on this (this could arguably be untrue if non-coding tasks are expected to completely dominate future OpenAI revenue in the short term, but even then, given what they pay for tokens vs. what I pay, it still seems like it would make sense for them to speed a lot of these things up given that I could do it outside of a lab; perhaps there's some kind of argument like, if you have access to their usage data, there are so many more important bottlenecks that this one doesn't make sense to prioritize, but it still seems like it should make sense for them at some point even if it doesn't fall into the top 100 bottlenecks for Cerebras-enabled coding agents). Another kind of thing that one might not call ambitious, but that speaks to the kind of thing that's possible, are games that I've made. There are games I've thought about and wanted to make that I don't think are generally enjoyable enough that they make sense for a real audience, but that I've wanted to play. For example, ever since reading David Gerrold's Star Wolf books in the 90s, I've wanted to play a game that implements combat as described in the books, which is a sort of like submarine combat. At least among realistic war games, this genre is extremely niche because almost everybody finds naval combat boring, and submarine combat is a particularly boring subgenre of naval combat games, so this doesn't really make sense as a money-making game, but it's so easy to implement games that I had an agent implement the game so I could play it for an hour or two. I never would've spent 10-20 hours implementing a game so that I could play it for an hour or two, but I'd spend 5 minutes. I've also previously mentioned implementing a game with the same rules as Scout and Guards of Atlantis 2 and other board games. I was never going to take the time to implement these games by hand just so I have a way to play with my friends on the occasions where we can't get together in-person, but I'm happy to have an LLM bash these things out. And, of course, for people who want to make games with a wider audience, there's a game renaissance going on right now due to coding agents. It's amazing how many interesting and creative games are being made now that having programming skills and the time to put them to use is no longer a bottleneck for making games. Data analysis is another thing where the productivity multiplier can be very high and I can do all sorts of things I never would've done. As I've mentioned in a number of my last posts, I have way too many of these projects to really be able to write them up, even when attempting to write very quickly and bash out posts in half an hour apiece. When I've talked to people about their one-off tooling, there's a lot of fun stuff people have done. For example, here's something Peter Geoghegan mentioned a month or two back: I had Fable implement a custom Neovim Lua function that formats code according to my very specific preferences. This is both something I don't want to maintain myself and inherently a Rube Goldberg device. Theoretically I could accomplish the same outcome in a principled way by patching clang-format, but my requirements are so exact that I think that approach would never be satisfactory. We use a tool call pgindent, which is our fork of bsd_indent. You can approximate the same formatting rules using clang-format, but that isn't good enough. If I commit something that isn't perfectly formatted/indented according to pgindent, I get a CI failure that I'm expected to fix quickly -- something I'd really prefer to avoid ... Practically speaking, getting slick, clang-format-style formatting that avoids nag emails about misindented code requires a total architectural mess (I also don't want to spend the time developing a principled approach, but that's really a separate issue). The function allows me to effortlessly format a given block of code from Neovim, similar to the clang-format LSP integration. I'm being unreasonably fussy here, of course, but I find that LLMs allow me to be this exacting about tooling. The function performs multiple passes: an initial formatting pass using clang-format/clangd, and a separate formatting pass using pgindent. I need it to do both because clang-format handles some cases correctly that pgindent misses. This is brittle because I only want to format the code within a range of lines selected via block visual mode (I don't want to run clang-format on code not added by my patch). This conflicts with pgindent's design; it can only format whole C files. Figuring out which relevant subset of the temp whole file buffer needs to be copied back into my working buffer is nontrivial. The initial line range I selected doesn't directly map to the affected C AST elements. So the function uses tree-sitter to intelligently delineate the exact subset of the temp indented C code that needs to be copied back. The rules need to be fuzzy in exactly the right way for cases where my selection straddles the same block of code. There are a bunch of edge cases. Another complicating factor is that pgindent relies on a typedef file generated with objdump to identify types; without that file, the formatting looks wonky. The formatting function dynamically generates any extra typedefs from clangd, for that one file, so I don't have to worry about a stale typedef file (I might have created a new struct seconds before running the formatting tool, I don't want to run objdump on the whole postgres binary each time, that'd blow up latency). This appears to work perfectly. The latency is totally acceptable. I have only a vague understanding of how all this works, though. I don't even know Lua. This will probably continue to work, even as further changes are made to our fork of bsd_indent that somewhat alter how code is formatted, which happens from time to time. I'm skeptical of the saaspocalypse. But I do think that LLMs are writing a lot of useful software that would have been insanely uneconomical to write any other way. There's an interesting small subset of software that'd be impossibly tedious for any human to maintain, relative to the value that it creates. I also caught with Malis while writing this and found out about all sorts of fun stuff he's been doing. It's enough that writing it all up in detail could be its own post, but one fun thing is that, the last time I taked to him about pgrust verification, he mentioned using Kani to verify some parts of the code. He's since switched to Lean and has been using Lean to verify things that are too complex to do in Kani. This would be another topic for another post, but I wonder why people have generally settled on Lean for LLM-driven proofs (as opposed to, say, ACL2 ). I wonder how Lean would look in an updated version of this theorem prover comparison , or if someone were to run a theorem prover eval that's analogous to this language eval . Of course, you can think of plenty of examples out of AI labs, such as a mid-sized team Anthropic building an internal replacement for GitHub as well as some other tooling in five months A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. I think these kinds of examples are interesting and they point to where the industry will be in the not-so-far future, but what you can do with unlimited tokens, while relying on other infrastructure and tooling built with unlimited tokens doesn't tell you much about what you can accomplish today without unlimited funds. Projects like pgrust as well as projects that people I know do in their spare time (of which I've probably mentioned something like 1%—there are just a lot of these, like David Turner creating an skipper for podcasts that's "works for me" quality that works better than anything he could find, the spare-time projects Dennis Snell mentioned here , etc.) are more representative of what you can do today. In this post, we're going to use ambitious in a way that feels consistent to me, but that one could argue is overloaded. I'm using this to mean, doing more than you could've before, in a generic sense. One could say that there's a difference between building a project that's larger than was reasonably feasible before and building some kind of super-specialized tool that could've been done before but just wasn't worth the time to build. While these are very different things, I think they both fall out of the same thing (it being much easier to produce software), so I feel pretty comfortable with this arguably overloaded definition. [return] Alex Kolovsky pointed out that these were not considered a bug. I see the argument from a security standpoint and I don't have enough context on Postgres to weigh on on this specifically, but I'll say that, for projects I've worked on, I've liked eliminating this kind of issue because it's a lot easier to find real bugs if you try to make your code clean from all issues like this. [return] One reason I trust Malis is that he's a lot more careful about what he claims than a stereotypical founder. For example, when I joined the pgrust discord to check out what people are saying, I saw this message from Malis (dated a month ago, 2026-09-17, an eternity in agentic coding land) in response someone asking about pgrust's readiness for use as a production database: I would not recommend using it as your primary production database today. We are setting a production deployment for a company right now, but they are more tolerant to their production database going down than most people. We'll have good empirical evidence on how reliable pgrust is after they start running it Malis doesn't seem like someone who would claim something is production ready when it's clearly wildly unready , like many well-known projects have, and it turns out he's not doing that. I wrote the draft of this a week before publishing and didn't have time to publish it. Since then, there was this pgrust Clickhouse benchmark controversy . On looking into this, the accusations of nefarious cheating seem to be false, and the accusation that it was premature to submit the preview of pgrust to the benchmark is something Malis acknowledged. I do think this is the kind of thing that a project will never live down, in that regardless of the truth of the matter, people will be bringing this up years later. You can see this right now in discussions around that specific controversy, and as we discussed when we look at Ed Zitron's prediction track record and when we looked at futurist predictors like Kurzwil , almost nobody actually looks at what actually happened and people will repeat incorrect statements that were based on vibes indefinitely. I don't think I can really present all of the evidence for why I trust Malis (technically, I could do it, but it would easily be a 20k+ word post), but if you look at how he discusses pgrust vs. how typical database founders market their new DB projects, it seems dramatically different to me. Of course there are extreme examples like MongoDB, which disputed correctness issues for years despite Kyle Kingsbury repeatedly showing that the anecdotes people had about data corruption were real. For an example that's more typical, a friend of mine worked as an early employee for a database startup. Their webpage bragged about doing some huge number of QPS. On testing it, my friend found that the claim was off by multiple orders of magnitude and suggested that the webpage get changed. The founder disagreed because they were going to hit the performance numbers, so it was still a true claim. After multiple years of performance improvements, the company eventually reduced the claim by one order of magnitude and they can still only hit that number with a very contrived, unrealistic, workload. This is, unfortunately, pretty normal for a company peddling a product based on its performance. By contrast, when I look at the pgrust discord to see what Malis is saying about performance, here's his most recent message: Right now, the best way to help is to find bugs and performance issues in 0.4-beta. The new query engine is very fast on some workloads, but it causes performance regressions on others, and it doesn't support some more complex queries. We're trying to track down everything that's either slower than Postgres or errors out. It's not an easy thing to do given the massive space of queries you can run We want to fix these things before the general release of 0.4-beta. Off the top of my head, there was a big performance regression in very fast queries. This is because we primarily optimized the new query engine for large-scale OLAP-like workloads. I'm doing optimization work to fix the very slow queries. I don't think there's any fundamental reason why the new engine should be slower than the previous one for fast queries Even though he was a founder and exec of a successful startup prior to starting the pgrust project, he never really got into the mindset that most founders seem to, where they seem to be able to say anything and believe anything they say. You might say this is a low bar, and I'd agree, but I still think it's rare and it's why I trusted what he says about pgrust without looking into it and also why, when I looked into it, his claims seem to be borne out by reality. [return] Another way to look at it is [this framing from Thomas Ptacek]: The last year in the technology industry has felt like 100 years all happening at once. Our industry is destabilized in a way nobody’s experienced since the advent of the personal computer. Every limit AI runs up against collapses within a month. Everything we do with frontier models today, in a few years we’ll be doing instantaneously and for free. Given the pace of change recently, I find it understandable that most people, even most programmers, aren't quite aware of what's possible right now. Speaking to non-programmer responses, one of the things I thought was interesting was how many people objected to this review of Ed Zitron's prediction accuracy because they thought that AI capabilities hadn't increased in the past two years. For most people I talk to, the idea that AI didn't improve from February 2024 to September 2026 is baffling (even if you think of programming as an exception and look at other capabilities), but there's a lot of people out there who are perhaps looking at the Google AI summary at the top of search results or using Copilot integrated into some Microsoft suite, who don't realize that capabilities have advanced. At every scale, there seems to be an information gradient like this, where very few people outside of labs have a good idea of what productive people are doing with models today. [return] This comment about an increase in cheating online has come to pass . On re-reading the actual comment that I wrote, I didn't explicitly write that it seemed inevitable that there would be a large increase in cheating, although it can be inferred from connecting the statements there together, and I've been on the record in public on some discords, etc. I don't follow the online game scene, but I'm told that for Azul (the most popular game on BGA, the biggest online board game platform for modern board games), 3 of the top 10 places last season were taken by cheaters, including top place. Also, as I've noted elsewhere in the past, BGA doesn't seem equipped to make reasonable policy decisions on almost any level. Things like the mechanics of their Elo ranking algorithm, their structure for game seasons, their policy for counteracting collusion, their policy for countering cheating, etc., are worse than the most naive straightforward solution you can think of so, as expected, they don't have a reasonable policy to counter cheating. The top ranks of the most popular game have been overrun with cheaters and this should be expected to spread to other games. As harms from AI go, this is a fairly benign one. It just happens to be one of a double-digit number of examples I saw last week of people being more ambitious in the software they create. I'm half mentioning this because it's easily quantifiable, and half because I predicted this would happen and it seems reasonable to follow up and see what happened. One side effect of people being more ambitious with the software they build is a rise in cheaters, scammers, and the like. On the bright side, when it comes to board games, perhaps six months ago, I made the comment on a board game discord that there isn't really any reason to play games on Board Game Arena over some vibe coded app because the vibe coded app will have better performance, be less buggy, have things like a move timer policy that actually makes sense, etc., unless the game is something like Guards of Atlantis 2, where the rules are so poorly written that AI struggles to understand the rules. At the time, I was already playing games with friends on apps I vibe coded (legally, as game rules and mechanics aren't copyrighted), but people thought I was a madman when I said this. Since then, I've seen a number of other people build their own apps so they can play a better implementation of a board game than is publicly available. I would rate every board game I've implemented as fairly bad, but in the pre-coding agent world, most online board games were even worse. In a coding variant of this argument , the bar to displace old human-written code isn't very high because most old human written code is atrocious. I suspect people playing these new vibe coded implementations actually better for board game designers since people playing their games more means more physical game sales, although I think people would do this regardless of whether or not it benefits board game designers because the existing verisons of so many games are really terrible. For example, if two players click at the same time in a game on BGA, this is an error, which is absurd for an online game platform. But BGA won because it's much better than the alternatives, and it's also better than most custom implementations (e.g., see the reviews for online Brass: Birmingham , where the game actually doesn't work). [return] BTW, this makes public evals not very meaningful for many use cases because what I and other programmers who are using models often care about is how good the model is at a task where the model still needs human guidance, not how good the model is at a task that's trivial for the model. [return] This is not a claim about the future. Perhaps almost all or perhaps even all of the software skills I have will become irrelevant in the near future. But we're not there yet. At the moment, programming skills seem higher leverage than ever before. There's something a bit funny about the current moment, where it seems like having the skills that models are replacing makes one much more effective than people who are trying to use models without having those skills. I like Max Bittker's framing that models are very good at counterfeiting and the level of expertise it takes to distinguish a counterfeit from the real thing has been increasing as models improve. title: In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn't Real
body_text: In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn’t Real Account Log in Subscribe Navigation Home About RSS Support/FAQ Podcast FOIA Forum Archive Merch Advertise Privacy Contact Us/Tips Follow us Twitter Bluesky Mastodon Instagram TikTok Facebook RSS Sign in Subscribe About RSS Support/FAQ Podcast FOIA Forum Archive Merch Advertise Privacy Contact Us/Tips Advertisement • Go ad free Flock In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn’t Real Joseph Cox , Jason Koebler · Oct 26, 2026 at 1:43 PM In comments at a private police conference, Garrett Langley also said his wife advised him to never apologize. IMAGE: SPUMONI COOPERATIVE FOR 404 MEDIA. Garrett Langley, the CEO of automatic license plate reader company Flock, told an audience of police chiefs at a private police conference Sunday that anti-Flock protests around the country are not real, according to leaked audio obtained by 404 Media. He also said his wife advised him to never apologize, said he would prefer to never do interviews with the press again, and claimed without evidence that the social media opposition to Flock is driven mostly by Russian bots. “Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley said about the many viral posts criticizing his company’s technology. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things,’” he added, repeating a disproven theory that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers had a significant impact on internet bot activity.  “It’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real,” he continued. “Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.” Langley’s comments echo another unsubstantiated theory that said opposition to Flock comes from a far-left network spreading propaganda at the behest of China . Langley made the comments at the International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP) conference, which is running Saturday to Tuesday in Orlando, Florida. Many law enforcement contractors exhibit at the conference, and speakers get to attend with more than 16,000 public safety officials . 0:00 / 1:39 1× Flock makes automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and other surveillance cameras. Its ALPRs constantly scan the license plate, color, make, and model of every vehicle that drives past, creating a timestamped log of peoples’ movements. The embattled company has faced extensive media and public scrutiny as instances of police abuse, false arrests, and the use of the technology for immigration enforcement have come to light. Dozens of cities have canceled their contracts with Flock over the last 18 months.  As backlash to the company grew, Langley began doing damage control with the media, which included apologizing for calling DeFlock, a group that maps the location of Flock cameras, a “ terroristic organization .” In the audio from the IACP conference, Langley suggested that he generally should not apologize for the company. 💡 Do you know anything else about Flock? We would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message Joseph securely on Signal at joseph.404, or Jason on jason.404 “I give my wife a lot of credit. She was, like, you should never apologize,” Langley said. “Sure, people make mistakes. I've made a lot of mistakes in the last nine years. I made a lot of mistakes this summer. But we do good work.” The session itself was framed as a fireside chat between Langley and David Rausch, IACP’s president and director of the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. The schedule said the session would “examine the opportunities, challenges, and public debate surrounding the technology [ALPRs], including issues related to privacy, transparency, governance, data use, and community trust.”  Never apologize 0:00 / 119.844 1× Flock makes the ALPR data available to its law enforcement customers, who can query it without a warrant. Flock differentiates itself from other ALPR providers, like Axon, by providing a national network of ALPRs. A cop in one part of the U.S. can search cameras not just in their own jurisdiction, or even state, but all over the country, if those other police departments have added their cameras to the network. A recent count put the national network at around 80,000 cameras. That national network is a large part of why Flock has faced so much criticism. 404 Media revealed last year that local cops were doing lookups in Flock for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and a cop in Texas searched cameras nationwide for a woman who self-administered an abortion. Langley said he’d like to not do any more media interviews. “The media gets to say whatever they want to say about you,” he said.  “I’d like to never do media again if that's possible. I don’t know if any chiefs can tell me. I’m going to try to figure this out but I think for me, I wish we could do this more often and you know I’m excited about the work we’re doing together and think we have a lot of ideas to continue to make up,” Langley said.  404 Media’s investigations on Flock and others have triggered a nationwide conversation about whether individual communities want Flock cameras stationed on their roads or inside their children' s gymnastics class . Flock is basically a meme on TikTok and Instagram now, with many creators trying to tell others about what the cameras do and the issues they raise (with varying accuracy, and some people making videos purely for the grift ). Some people have even taken to vandalizing, destroying, or reverse-engineering Flock cameras , with the government monitoring anti-Flock social media accounts. That nationwide conversation has now reached the Hill, with multiple lawmakers proposing legislation that would ban or otherwise dramatically rein in Flock. Flock competitor Axon threw a party at the Hard Rock Cafe on Sunday night, according to the conference schedule. Flock did not respond to a request for comment. Langley suggested during the session with Rausch that eventually the opposition to Flock will die down: “Whenever this industry finds a highly effective tool, it has to go through this period of intense debate. But then you get on the other side. I think right now we’re not at the bottom, but we’re real, dang, near close to it and about to come back up on the other side.” About the author Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. title: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs
body_text: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs | Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist Charlie Gerard Projects Speaking Blog Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs 20/10/2026 I was doing a little creative exercise the other day around the word "Overgrowth". The first thing that came to mind was an apocalyptic scene, something like The Walking Dead or The Last of Us, where plants tend to overgrow abandoned buildings. I then wanted to apply this idea to the digital world, and the word "abandoned" made me think of my browser tabs... What if my tabs were slowly taken over by plants the longer I left them unread? What if I had to clear away these invasive plants to access my tabs again? A bit like trying to open a door that's been overgrown... So I built this fun little Chrome extension that does just that. It won't necessarily make me read my tabs more but it's ok. Demo Link to the repository The idea Every tab has a neglect clock. It runs while the tab is out of view and stops while you're looking at it. The longer a tab is neglected, the more plants grow over it, from the edges towards the middle. Once a tab is more than 5% overgrown, the page behind the vines is walled off: you can scroll, but you can't click, select or drag anything. To free it, you have to slash through the vines by dragging your mouse across them. Get it down to 5% and the last bits fall off. If you abandon your tab once more, the jungle starts growing again. Just for fun, you can pick your weapon of choice between the rusty machete, the chainsaw and the flamethrower. You can also change how long it takes for your tabs to be fully overgrown. Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying... 😅 The extension The code is organised in 3 main parts: the background logic, the content script to display the plants and animation on the tabs and the popup folder that handles the UI of the extension itself. Background worker The background.js file starts the jungle on each open tab and forgets it when it closes. The popup This folder handles the UI for the extension with some small components for the time setting, the weapon choice, the list of tabs and their current stat. The overlay The content folder contains the SVGs for the plants and the weapons, the logic to position and grow the clusters, the neglect clock and the sounds. I've been wanting to get back into building things for a while now and this project felt like a small, fun way to start. I'm writing this on a new computer so I currently "only" have 22 tabs open but 14 of them are already completely overgrown... 😂 It might not make me read them more but slashing through the vines makes coming back to them more fun! 🪚🌿

title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
body_text: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why? | Max Woolf's Blog Skip to content Max Woolf's Blog Posts Search GitHub   Patreon   OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why? October 25, 2026  ·  12 min Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok . June 26, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50 , while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10 . They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it. June 30, 2026 # Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up. July 24, 2026 # Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed. July 30, 2026 # OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02 . Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI August 10, 2026 # Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent. August 21, 2026 # OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ( $4 / $20 / $0.40 ) for the next three months. September 1, 2026 # Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%. Cache read costs When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote! September 3, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable. September 22, 2026 # OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version. On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post). September 29, 2026 # It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper. Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code . More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts. Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost. However, aggregate spend has been increasing because the models are getting better faster than they’re getting cheaper! via Vercel From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives? The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure # If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent , or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter , and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta —who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure. For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1 , which also recently released an updated 1017 variant . OpenRouter at this point is the place you go for open-weight models. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise ( 45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24 ) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003 . Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”. On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers . Providers for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sorted by cache read cost. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise. Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost. Despite the fact that these models are the cheapest, note that these models only have a minority of the total token share. Retrieved October 24th, 2026. OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58 ) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ( $2 / $10 / $0.20 ). It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price. Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ( $3 / $15 / $0.30 ). One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends. The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s , but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high. As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more . It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet . The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic. As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too. The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost. On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts. IPO Pumping # The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon— OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months . So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months. Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around. So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%? That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus! The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats. How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts? Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave. I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets . Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did? I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice. In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models. For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing. I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon. I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models. After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good. Top-and-left. via Anthropic I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced. Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it. One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures. However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline. Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining! Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct. Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die. I am a former Data Scientist of 9 years currently seeking a job in data science/machine learning/AI in-person in the San Francisco Bay Area, ideally within San Francisco proper. If you found my writing interesting and you’re interested, please let me know at max[at]minimaxir.com ! Max Woolf (@minimaxir) is formerly a Senior Data Scientist at BuzzFeed in San Francisco who works with AI/ML tools and open source projects. Max’s projects are funded by his Patreon .
