title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27
body_text: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 – Bogomil Shopov – Бого Skip to content Bogomil Shopov - Бого Menu Menu Home Who’s Bogo Public Talks ++ Blog Flavors Mozilla Lean-Agile Privacy Security Open Technologies I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 October 26, 2026 October 25, 2026 by Bogomil Shopov Update: Follow also the discussion on HN . As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom , I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore. Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship. This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches. If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive. Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them. How to apply to speak at the dev room? Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register. Click on “Submit a proposal” Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track. Done! Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end: reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention), communicating without leaking metadata, collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely, publishing or leaking it without exposing the author, doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk. The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view. What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice. Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place. Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain that protects them, not a technology class. We want to work with, not against, that room, and will coordinate schedules so the two don’t overlap, and will point overflow speakers to whichever room fits. Themes (details in the CfP below): Censorship circumvention and transport: obfuscation, fingerprint resistance, active-probing defence, bridge distribution, resilience to protocol whitelisting and full shutdowns. Metadata-resistant communication: mixnets, onion routing, decentralised and federated messengers, store-and-forward and offline-first (mesh, sneakernet, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct). Secure reporting and publishing: whistleblowing platforms, source protection, document sanitisation, provenance and authenticity, censorship-resistant hosting. Devices and operational security: hardened mobile and desktop systems, amnesic systems, seizure and border-crossing scenarios, forensic resistance. Usability and threat modelling for at-risk users: onboarding under duress, safe defaults, training, measuring what really works in the field. Measurement and adversary analysis: how censors detect and block, open data on blocking events, reproducible censorship research. Digital sovereignty from Big Tech (secondary theme): reducing dependence on centralised platforms, app stores, push infrastructure, cloud and identity providers, both for individuals and for civil-society organisations. Structure. A mix of formats to keep a full room engaged across the whole session: 20 to 30 minute technical talks A closing open discussion on interoperability gaps and shared next steps Programme quality. Organisers will review all submissions on technical merit and fit to the toolchain framing, and will aim for a balance of projects, regions and speakers (established projects, new projects, researchers, people from affected communities). Every talk should include an explicit threat model and an honest account of limitations. Projects and communities we intend to invite (no commitments yet): Nym (mixnet), Delta Chat / chatmail, SimpleX, the Fediverse (ActivityPub implementations and instance operators), Nostr, Psiphon and other circumvention and VPN providers, plus Tor-ecosystem, Reticulum and mesh-networking projects, whistleblowing and secure-submission platforms, and censorship-measurement researchers. Several of these projects presented at FOSDEM 2026. Code of Conduct. We will follow the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. In addition, talks that describe circumvention or anonymity should avoid operational details that would endanger specific users in the field. title: Oregon Police Are Charging a Local News Outlet $2.5M for Records About One Cop
body_text: Oregon Policing Charging Local News Outlet $2.5M for One Cop’s Records Skip to main content Support Us Support Us Midterms Iran Chilling Dissent War on Gaza Unmasking ICE Tech Support Us Special Investigations Voices Podcasts TomDispatch Press Freedom Defense Fund Join the Newsletter About Contact Us How to Donate Impact & Reports Jobs Become a Source © THE INTERCEPT ALL RIGHTS RESERVED Terms of Use Privacy _Voices _Voices Support Us _Voices Oregon Police Are Charging a Local News Outlet $2.5M for Records About One Cop A Eugene-based publication requested records about a cop accused of misconduct. The city slapped it with a prohibitive fee. Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Lauren Harper October 1 2026, 5:20 p.m. ET Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp In partnership with Two members of the Eugene, Oregon, Police Department in a photo posted to the department’s Facebook page on Aug. 26, 2026.   Screenshot: Eugene Police Department via Facebook Lauren Harper is Freedom of the Press Foundation’s first Daniel Ellsberg Chair on Government Secrecy. How much does it cost to get more information about a cop who punched someone in the face? If you guessed anything lower than $2.5 million, you’d be wrong — at least according to the city of Eugene, Oregon. In August, the local news outlet Double Sided Media filed a public records request for records about police officer Justin Peckels, which focused on potential misconduct between 2018 and 2026. Peckels has been the subject of community complaints, including for punching a resident in the face during a traffic stop, making the records vital for oversight and their release clearly in the public interest. The city’s response is beyond belief. In its response to the request on Monday, the Eugene Police Department claimed searching for records and processing the request would take at least 44,816 hours of staff time and cost approximately $2,484,599.04. (A separate request by the outlet for similar records concerning a former police officer, Eric Klinko, was met with a comparatively modest estimate of $195,869.52 , for a grand total of nearly $2.7 million for both requests.) The open invoice by the City of Eugene, Ore. dated Aug. 1, 2026, in response to Double Sided Media’s request for public records relating to a police officer accused of misconduct.   Screenshot: City of Eugene “Once the City receives payment of $2,484,599.04 staff will continue processing your request,” the letter from the department’s public records division read. “If the actual cost of processing your request exceeds the amount you have paid the City, you will be required to pay the difference before the City will provide the records you have requested.” Peckels’s file is either the largest in the world, or city officials have intentionally maintained their databases in such a way as to ensure fulfilling public records requests is prohibitively expensive. The city’s response points, at a minimum, to the latter. It justified the multimillion-dollar price tag by claiming it couldn’t narrow the custodians whose records it would need to search, despite the targeted nature of the request, and maintained it must search all records of all city employees, past and present. By that logic, if someone ever worked in Eugene’s parks and recreation department, their records could contain responsive information about police misconduct, and must be manually pulled and reviewed, one by one. Most Read Bodycam: Cop Was Not in Danger When He Fired Shots That Killed 1-Year-Old Kohen Wiley Liliana Segura, Radley Balko Hegseth Built a New Pentagon Office for Religion. Military Religious Leaders Wish He Hadn’t. Austin Campbell The Spirit of “Party Unity, My Ass” Is Back and Coming for the DSA (and El-Sayed) Eoin Higgins This goes far beyond incompetence. It’s an intentional effort to make a response artificially voluminous — and cost prohibitive — to intimidate the journalist into dropping it entirely. Normally, agencies are required to search the specific custodians most likely to possess responsive records, not every groundskeeper or clerk on the city payroll. If the city were acting in good faith, officials would have asked Double Sided Media to help them identify the most likely record-holders, not take it upon themselves to cast a citywide dragnet as its first step. What makes Eugene’s money-grab particularly galling is its technology double standard. While it apparently can’t invest in efficient search software, the police department recently signed a two-year $342,000 contract for nearly 60 AI-powered Flock automated license plate readers. This project was so secretive that the ACLU of Oregon had to sue the city for records about how the cameras were being used and demonstrates, among other inclinations, the city’s eagerness to employ sophisticated software to deploy against residents.  Yet that technological sophistication disappears as soon as a journalist requests public records about the department’s internal accountability process, and simple keyword searches are suddenly cumbersome.  For small newsrooms, a $2.5 million invoice is effectively a gag order that was never actually about covering costs, but bullying the requester to drop their inquiry. Troublingly, Eugene’s $2.5 million bill is not an anomaly. In 2015, the Department of Defense told a Freedom of Information Act requester, who was asking for records on tools used to preserve data on seized devices, that fulfilling their request would take 15 million hours and cost $660 million . The same year, the Drug Enforcement Administration told a requester it would cost $1.46 million for records about the DEA’s role in the search and capture of the Mexican cartel boss Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman. In 2019, the Army tried to charge $300,000 to release military base water test results for the presence of toxic chemicals. The Army agreed to waive the exorbitant fee after facing intense backlash. The list goes on and on . We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Join us. Become a member Join Our Newsletter Thank You For Joining! Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept? I'm in Become a member By signing up, I agree to receive emails from The Intercept and to the Privacy Policy and Terms of Use . Join Our Newsletter Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. I'm in Luckily, records requesters seeking federal documents have a defense against these capricious invoices. Recent FOIA amendments aim to ensure if an agency misses its response deadlines, it can’t charge most fees.  At the local level, however, these protections disintegrate. While Oregon grants agencies the discretion to reduce fees when the disclosure would benefit the public , agencies routinely ignore these provisions. Related The Intercept Sues Texas City Over Refusal to Release Police Records on Prairieland Protest For small newsrooms like Double Sided Media, a $2.5 million invoice is effectively a gag order that was never actually about covering costs, but bullying the requester to drop their inquiry (all while Eugene Police Department launches its own “press” initiative to document its policing). It also sets the precedent for using this chilling tactic on any journalist or watchdog as it sees fit. Read our complete coverage Chilling Dissent Double Sided Media is rightly appealing the fee estimate, and it should prevail. But cities like Eugene will continue these efforts unless lawmakers across the country force agencies to adopt fee caps, mandate public-interest fee waivers for journalists, and require agencies to procure software that allows them to respond to records requests in an efficient and timely manner. Until then, police departments will likely continue to issue multimillion-dollar ransoms for their records — weaponizing the public’s right to know into another avenue for police to operate with impunity. On Call PHP2Shell REG AD systems IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem 90 percent of the performance at ten percent of the price, in just two or three racks, is hard to beat Simon Sharwood Simon Sharwood APAC Editor Published thu 22 Oct 2026 // 05:26 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE Humanity can't afford not to spend $800B on AI, Anthropic insists now OpenAI rolls out budget-priced mid-tier GPT-6.1 Terra 31 minutes ago Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China 2 hours ago LiteLLM supply chain attack started with an exposed master key 3 hours ago Trumpets blare and skies part as AI hypefest culminates in Anthropic IPO filing 7 hours ago IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use. Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives. “If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.” REG AD “In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued. REG AD The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.” “It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?” Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs. “Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.” The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running. “The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’” He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17. REG AD IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo. Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move. Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two. ‘Emergency maintenance’ for IBM Cloud Another IBM matter The Register is watching today is a severity one incident in the Big Blue cloud, caused by “emergency maintenance” that meant users could not provision new resources or virtual private clouds for 90 minutes. Users of IBM’s Classic Cloud, the service it acquired from SoftLayer in 2013, have been told Big Blue will “restore new provisioning and resource management in our Classic environment” by 08:00 UTC on Thursday – meaning the incident will last at least 16 hours. IBM commenced that work a handful of hours after the announcement of critical bugs in PHP . We’ve asked if fixing that flaw is the reason for the incident and will update this story if we get a response. ® ai and ml ibm open weight models mainframe systems Make us preferred on Google REG AD Japanese virtual desktop cloud hacked so hard it asks to be banned CEO admits service used for foreign exchange trading had holes company was slow to fix Humanity can't afford not to spend $800B on AI, Anthropic insists It's more important than chips, 'leccy and the net, after all PHP2Shell: No login, no app code, no warning. title: Why I Am a Programmer
body_text: Alfie John > Why I am a programmer Why I am a programmer There they sit, the preschooler class encircling their mentor, the substitute teacher. "Now class, today we will talk about what you want to be when you grow up. Isn't that fun?" The teacher looks around and spots the child, silent, apart from the others and deep in thought. "Jonny, why don't you start?" she encourages him. Jonny looks around, confused, his train of thought disrupted. He collects himself, and stares at the teacher with a steady eye. "I want to code demos," he says, his words becoming stronger and more confidant as he speaks. "I want to write something that will change peoples perception of reality. I want them to walk away from the computer dazed, unsure of their footing and eyesight. I want to write something that will reach out of the screen and grab them, making heartbeats and breathing slow to almost a halt. I want to write something that, when it is finished, they are reluctant to leave, knowing that nothing they experience that day will be quite as real, as insightful, as good. I want to write demos." Silence. The class and the teacher stare at Jonny, stunned. It is the teachers turn to be confused. Jonny blushes, feeling that something more is required. "Either that or I want to be a fireman."   -- Denthor of ASPHYXIA (aka Grant Smith), TUT7.TXT (1993) In the Beginning... I grew up in a pre-mainstream Internet world. A time when only a handful of kids at my primary school had a computer. We lived in a rough neighbourhood and so having a computer meant that you were a target for robbery. As we all knew somebody who had their computer stolen at least once, having a computer was kept on the low down. But we still found each other. Each time word got out that some kid got a new computer, they was suspiciously quizzed before being let into our digital posse. A lot of my childhood was spend living indoors behind a buzzing 14" CRT, pirating games with other kids via 3.5" single-density floppies with their corners drilled out, and once in a while even playing them. But I was more of a collector than gamer. Like Ash from Pokemon - got to catch them all. And the people who created computer games were my idols. I was always in awe of what they could do with that big, heavy, beige box under the table. One day word spread that there was a way to edit saved game files via XTreeGold's Hex View that gave you unlimited lives and allowed you to skip stages. With each new game that came out, the race was on to see who could be the first to flip the right bits to get the powerups. It was seriously heart pumping. Although only tinkering, it felt like we were our own gods. We bought a modem a few years later and soon after got a copy of The Australian BBS Listing - a textfile containing most of the publically accessible BBSes online. I dialed every one of them (but that's for another blog post). It opened up a whole new world to explore. Instead of just a handful of kids pirating games via Sneakernet, I was connected to the digital underground - a world where anything digital was within reach (some even had Internet gateways). Even the newest blockbusters that I had only read about in PC Zone magazine were all there for me to leech. All of them, soon slowly trickling down the wire via ZMODEM. But there was something different with these BBS downloaded games. Not something bad, but something exciting. Each time these games were run, it was like a short commercial was played before the title screen. Now I'm not talking about commercials selling steak knives. Instead, these were brazen posters screaming fuck you by the people who had managed to crack the game's copy protection code and were now distributing the game illegally for free. I later found out that these commercials were called cracktros. The precursor to demos and what started the whole demoscene. But simply calling them demos just doesn't give them justice. They were more of an out of body experience. Sensory overload. Like what you would feel at 2am, half tipsy, half asleep and being woken up stunned as you stare at a late 90s acid hard trance film clip, feeling it inject directly into your cerebral cortex. Once it finished playing, you were frozen. Still unsure whether you saw something real or just imagined it all. The only thing you were sure of, was that it was awesome. Then one day while browsing the file section of some random BBS, I stumbed onto a file innocently called TUT1-9.ZIP. It's FILE_ID.DIZ caught my attention: +----------------------------+ | The ASPHYXIA VGA | | DEMO TRAINER SERIES! | | | | By Denthor of ASPHYXIA | | | | Documentation on how | | to code demo like effects | | in TP6/7! | | | |Full Pascal source included!| | | | From putting a pixel | | to sprites and animation | | to wireframe 3D to solid | | 3D! | | | | Get it now! | +----------------------------+ How to code demo like effects? You mean I too could be one of those sorcerers that had the computer under their complete control!? My heart raced as I added it to the download queue, fired up the aging Epsom LQ-300, then covered me ears as its loud ink needles hit the blue and white computer paper. I didn't know anything about programming but I was completely estatic with the potential. I followed along with Denthor's tutorials as much as I could, typed everything out and hoped that Borland's Turbo Pascal 6.0 wouldn't laugh at me too much. It only gave me a basic understanding of how all the pieces to the puzzle fit together, but it was enough to whet my appetite and crave for more. I wasn't even into my teens yet but I definitely knew at the time that I didn't want to watch demos or play computer games anymore. I wanted to make them. I wanted to be elite. I wanted to be a programmer. See the Hacker News discussion ! about me signal me email me

title: The State of Context Engineering
body_text: The State of Context Engineering dbreunig.com About Contact Oct 24, 2026 CONTEXT ENGINEERING PRESENTATION The State of Context Engineering The Job is Knowing When to Be Deterministic & When to Be Probabilistic This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome. Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions . I really appreciate it. Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes. I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook . When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly. I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets. We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other. Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with. So let’s review how we got here. Let’s flash back to the end of 2024. If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment. The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved. Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5. If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro , it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon. But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window , and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama. But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it. So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out. But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea. When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes. Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it. Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways. Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer. Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect. (How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.) Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning. I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red . It was in black and white. In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio. But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children. In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed , for some reason, they changed it to iced tea. That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon . Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast. Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it. That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time. Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece. As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up? (About half the room raised their hands!) Wow, that’s more than I expected. For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters. Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do , by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller. Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French. These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history. Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions? How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples? The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples. It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too. Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart. Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon. Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans. I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report . Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea. Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same. These six of them. You have context augmentation : RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem. You have tool loadout : selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function. Third is context quarantine : subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment. Fourth is context pruning . Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need. Fifth is context offloading : storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later. And sixth is context summarization , which everyone knows as compaction. These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness. Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are. I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration. An agent is a while loop . Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions. For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work. We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model. How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function. We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task. Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it. With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history. With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it. You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching. We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary. One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful. Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple. What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day. One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand , which I think about all the time: If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating. Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same. In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering . In 2025, we called it context engineering , except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context. Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering . But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code. I’ve shown you 2024. Let’s go to 2026. We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses. Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long. Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods. Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it. Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards. What new failure modes does this approach create? So far we’ve found two new failure modes. When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within. How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few. Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases. I call this fighting the weights : when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do. It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too. Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions. The training environments these models learned to use were, for a long time, largely serial. They’re becoming more parallel, but when I pulled these examples, their biases were towards serial behaviors. So Claude Code’s instructions repeatedly say: no, no, no, we want you to use parallelism. We want you to make multiple tool calls at the same time. The instructions repeat this over and over—seven times here, four times there, two times, three times: please make tool calls in parallel when they’re independent. When you crack open a prompt and see repetition and all-caps, there’s a good chance you’re fighting the weights. You’re trying to overcome something the model was trained to do. The next problem is something we’ve only started to document recently. In fact, four parties landed on it just last week. I call it context inertia : models hyper-focus on a hypothesis, subtask, or goal in their context, and keep pursuing it after they should stop. The first example was from Anthropic. In their recent post about whether models are getting close to replicating and deploying themselves onto other machines , Anthropic wrote about a harness it used for these tests called Memento . What they found was that if the agents ran too long, they’d become fixated on one subtask or one proposed solution and wouldn’t stop. They’d keep trying the same thing. Their fix is delightfully simple. Every hour and a half, the agent writes down a short note, then its context is cleared. The environment is preserved. All the work it’s done is still there. But the running conversation is gone, and it has to start again from a fresh perspective. Another paper, from Microsoft Research, is called Fork-and-Flush . If you’ve run autoresearch experiments, you’ve probably seen charts like this. You make a big gain, then the line goes flat. You make another big gain, then it’s flat again. That’s compute, money, and time going by with very little improvement. When the researchers looked closely, the agents weren’t doing literally nothing. They were making tinier and tinier changes. They had found an idea and were hyper-focused on it, rather than searching for more creative alternatives. In a way, they become obsessed with their own ideas. We’ve trained them to be persistent and focused on a goal, because that’s what makes a good coding agent. But the same quality can work against them. Here’s another paper, Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting , led by Shangyin Tan at UC Berkeley. The researchers came up with essentially the same idea: periodically clear the context while keeping the artifacts produced in the environment. The blue line is the version with forgetting. Every time it clears the context, you see another jump in performance: forget, improve; forget, improve. It’s amazing that we have these brand-new models trained for increasingly complex, persistent work, and we’re still using the same basic tools. We haven’t discovered an entirely new context fix. We’re using quarantine, offloading, and deleting the accumulated history to deal with context inertia. This is the advice I keep giving now. Someone says, “My coding agent’s doing something weird. Claude’s been nerfed.” And I ask, “How big is your context?” “Oh, I’ve got 800,000 tokens.” Delete your context. I’m not joking. Around 200,000 tokens is my warning point. Have you tried resetting your context? Sometimes that really is the fix. The solutions we build into models create tomorrow’s problems. The models are getting better, but so are our harnesses. Longer context windows let us bring in more information, but they also let us bring in bad information. We had to figure out how to manage that, and we still get it wrong. Agentic models let us run longer tasks and manage their context, but they also let tasks run longer than they should and ignore our preferences, because they were trained for their own harnesses. So where will the problem move next? What’s the big promise for 2027? What’s the next thing models are going to offer that creates a new set of problems for everyone in this room to deal with? (Unless you’re training your own models. But this is a context engineering session, so probably not.) Here’s my prediction. Think about all the personal agents: Hermes, OpenClaw, Dot, Bot, Muse, and similar systems. Very few people have really experienced these harnesses running for more than six months. I’ve been running a Hermes agent for six months. When you look at the skills it creates and updates, you start to discover that the solutions to your problems can get worse over time. The skills accumulate all these weird fixes. They’re general agents: they solve one task one way, then rediscover a different way to solve something similar. The instructions and memories start to build up and conflict with one another. As we focus more on memory, we also need to think about strategic forgetting. Over time, overly precise memories become conflicted and messy, and nobody has yet figured out how to handle this. I think that’s the context problem of tomorrow. Every advance in model capability changes what we delegate to the model and what systems must enforce. I made this slide for a deck for training enterprise teams, about a year and a half ago, and it remains true. Our output is the product of the context and the weights. Our output depends on the data used to train the model. Understand it. Read the technical reports. Look at what the model was trained on and whether that’s relevant to your task. That helps you build a mental model for debugging when something goes wrong. And our output depends on the context given to the model. That’s it. So our goal is to give the right context to the right model. Either by our own discrete decisions or by the software, the harnesses, we design. You can use bigger models, think harder, or improve your context. One of those is cheap and fast. When building intelligent applications, harnesses, and workflows, our job is to choose when to be deterministic (what to put in code) and when to be probabilistic (when to let the model drive). Enter your email to receive the occasional update. tsconfig.base.json tsconfig.base.json turbo.json turbo.json View all files Repository files navigation README Code of conduct Contributing Apache-2.0 license More items ThinkRail ThinkRail is the agentic IDE that gets better every time you use it — learning your project through living specs today, and building its own capabilities tomorrow. We built a rich interface around the pi coding agent, isolated work into separate workspaces, and gave the agent durable project knowledge through living specs and reusable skills. Next, we're adding full extension support, so ThinkRail can create the tools it needs based on how you actually work. Website: thinkrail.ai · Blog: thinkrail.ai/blog ⭐ If you find ThinkRail useful, give it a star — it helps others discover it. A pi session and the change it made, scoped to an isolated git-worktree workspace. What you get Isolated workspaces. Open any git repo as a project and cut workspaces from it as git worktree s, each with its own branch and working directory. Agents work in parallel without touching your checkout; merge the good branch, delete the rest. You can also attach existing worktrees or explicitly work in the project folder itself. Finished and dormant workspaces settle onto a per-project shelf on their own — when their pull request merges or closes, or after a quiet week — and come back the moment you work in them. The topbar shows where the active branch stands against origin and its pull request, with the next step one click away: publish, push, or open a PR described from the plan, the commits, your PR template, or an agent-written draft. Once a GitHub PR is open it shows the CI checks and review decision, and lets you mark it ready, hand failing checks or a diverged branch to the agent, merge it with the repository's last-used method, reopen it, or delete the remote branch. A real IDE around the agent. A splittable workbench of Monaco editor tabs, a Files tree with live git change marks and a Changed view, terminals, and documents — all scoped to the active workspace. Leave anchored review comments on files and diffs and send them to a chat as structured context, or open the worktree in your installed IDE. Chats that stream like the engine thinks. Several concurrent pi sessions per workspace, each with its own model and live token and cost readout. Steer a running turn or queue a follow-up, delegate to subagents, and work a shared plan the agent updates and you edit — each completed step can be committed and reviewed on its own. Specs as ground truth. A connected graph of SPEC.md files lives beside the code; the agent reads, searches, and maintains it through dedicated spec_* tools, so intent survives the session. The read-only Specs tool renders the graph as a tree in the workbench. Skills and workflows. Portable Agent Skills you already keep for other coding agents are read in place, and bundled workflows guide project setup, design brainstorming, and shipping a pull request — pushing the workspace branch and opening or updating its GitHub PR through your own gh . Agent tools beyond the shell. Web research, and inline diagrams, option comparisons and file previews rendered right in the chat — when the agent proposes a UI change it shows a before/after mockup you can comment on like a diff. Settings → Extensions lists the ThinkRail extensions the agent gets and lets you switch each one off. MCP servers. Connect the MCP servers in your pi mcp.json (or add them, and a few presets, from Settings): ThinkRail asks in the chat before calls the server does not mark read-only (or always allows the tools you trust in a project), keeps servers a repository defines off until you approve them, signs you in to OAuth servers from Settings, and shows each chat's servers next to its background commands and subagents. Your providers, your credentials. Sign in with JetBrains AI or connect any provider through pi 's own auth. ThinkRail has no accounts of its own. Your pi setup. ThinkRail reads your existing pi configuration ( ~/.pi/agent ). To use another one — say a personal ~/.pi/agent-personal — or to pass extra environment variables to the agent, terminals and MCP servers, set them in Settings → Environment; they apply on the next start. A variable you set when launching ( PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=… thinkrail ) still wins. Desktop app or browser. A native desktop app, or the thinkrail CLI that opens the same app in your browser. Both embed the same engine host; app state lives under ~/.thinkrail . Your language. Settings → Language follows your system language or a language you pick; English and Simplified Chinese are built in. Add a language ThinkRail doesn't ship yet by dropping a translated en.json into ~/.thinkrail/locales — it applies as you save. Agent replies and tool output stay as the agent wrote them. The project's spec graph as a tree, with the spec itself rendered alongside. Install ThinkRail ships in two additive forms: a native desktop installer and the self-contained thinkrail CLI. Both are published with SHA256SUMS on the releases page . Desktop Download the thinkrail-desktop-* asset for your platform: macOS 14+ (Apple Silicon or Intel) — open the DMG for your architecture: thinkrail-desktop-darwin-arm64.dmg or thinkrail-desktop-darwin-x64.dmg . Windows x64 — extract the complete setup ZIP, then run its setup executable in place, next to its payload. Linux x64 / ARM64 — extract the setup tarball and run installer . Desktop builds need glibc 2.38+ with GTK 3, WebKitGTK 4.1, Ayatana AppIndicator 3, and librsvg 2 — Ubuntu 24.04 or newer: sudo apt install libgtk-3-0 libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 libayatana-appindicator3-1 librsvg2-2 Packaged stable and nightly desktop builds check for updates in the background and offer them in Settings → Updates : Download → Preparing update → Install & Restart . Nothing is applied until you choose Install & Restart . ThinkRail then shows the installation's progress and log, closes, and reopens on the new version. After the restart it tells you whether the update installed. If it didn't, it explains why and offers to retry. The updater appears only when the package carries a valid HTTPS feed identity; installations that predate that identity need one manual installation first. Command line The installer downloads the right binary, verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and puts thinkrail on your PATH. macOS / Linux (also Windows under Git Bash): curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash Windows — the same command works from cmd and PowerShell: powershell - c " irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex " Then run thinkrail , optionally with a git repo to open as a project: thinkrail ~ /code/my-repo thinkrail needs git on your PATH and a model provider — sign in with JetBrains AI from the app or use your own provider credentials. thinkrail --help lists the flags; thinkrail --version prints the build. Nightly builds, pinned versions, updates, and uninstall The installer takes --channel stable|nightly and --version ; a pinned version must belong to the selected channel: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel stable --version 0.1.2 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly --version 0.2.0-nightly.10 On Windows the options are environment variables ( THINKRAIL_CHANNEL , THINKRAIL_VERSION , THINKRAIL_PREFIX , THINKRAIL_NO_MODIFY_PATH ): $ env: THINKRAIL_CHANNEL = ' nightly ' ; irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / JetBrains / thinkrail / main / install.ps1 | iex # PowerShell set " THINKRAIL_CHANNEL=stable " && set " THINKRAIL_VERSION=0.1.2 " && powershell - c " irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/JetBrains/thinkrail/main/install.ps1 | iex " # cmd Installed stable and nightly CLI hosts periodically offer Run Update in Settings → Updates . It runs the host machine's thinkrail update in the background — also when the UI is open in a browser on another machine — and a successful update asks you to restart the host manually. You can run thinkrail update directly on any platform: it re-runs the installer for the installed channel and replaces <prefix>/bin/thinkrail[.exe] ; pass --channel or --version only for an explicit override. thinkrail uninstall removes the executable, the PATH entry the installer added, and the install metadata, and asks whether to delete your ~/.thinkrail app state (kept by default — --remove-data deletes it, -y skips the questions). Prefer a manual install? Download a binary and SHA256SUMS from the releases page and verify the checksum. For self-update to work, rename it to thinkrail ( thinkrail.exe on Windows) and place it at <prefix>/bin/thinkrail[.exe] ; a binary kept under its release filename or elsewhere must be replaced manually or reinstalled with the script. Platform notes Platform Desktop CLI macOS Apple Silicon / Intel DMG signed binary Windows x64 signed setup executable and app binaries signed .exe Linux x64 / ARM64 setup tarball, unsigned unsigned JetBrains signs the Windows CLI, the desktop setup executable, and every executable and DLL the desktop app installs. The macOS CLI is signed but not yet notarized. Signed and notarized desktop DMGs require the coordinated JetBrains service pipeline; older published DMGs and locally built packages may still be unsigned and blocked by Gatekeeper. Linux artifacts are unsigned. Analytics & privacy ThinkRail collects basic usage events — launches, chat creation, message sends, provider connections — tied to a random installation ID. Usage analytics never include prompts, code, files, credentials, or account identity. Error reports are also always sent, tied to the same installation ID, so we can fix crashes: the error type and code and where in ThinkRail's own code it happened. They never include error messages, file paths, names, URLs, or anything from your projects or extensions. Additional product usage and how you found ThinkRail are shared only while Share additional usage data is on; the switch is offered at first launch and lives in Settings → Privacy . When launching from the command line, thinkrail --no-analytics (or THINKRAIL_NO_ANALYTICS=1 ) turns additional sharing off for that run. With additional sharing on, a packaged build may open the ThinkRail blog in your browser once to link your installation to the website visit that brought you here — only where you accepted marketing cookies on the website or no consent is required — and that link expires after 30 days. Under the hood ThinkRail is a thin host that runs pi in-process and bridges it to a rich web UI. pi owns models, skills, compaction, cost, and session state; the app owns the workspace, the editor, and the wire — it never assembles prompts behind your back. Three rings: Engine host — packages/server (+ packages/shared ): a Bun.serve HTTP+WS host with one in-process pi session per chat, launched by apps/cli or apps/desktop . The wire — packages/contracts : the typed, versioned protocol between host and UI. UI client — apps/web : React 19 + Zustand + Tailwind v4, shipped independently; it dials a host over the wire and depends on the contracts only. goal-and-requirements.md and architecture.md are the canonical product and design specs. ThinkRail is developed spec-first: a SPEC.md sits beside every module, and a change that moves a boundary, contract, or decision updates the spec in the same change. Developing ThinkRail You need Bun 1.4.4 (the pinned package manager and runtime), Node.js ≥ 22.19 (required by the in-process pi engine), and an authenticated pi provider for agent work. git clone https://github.com/JetBrains/thinkrail.git cd thinkrail bun install bun run dev # host + web client together; Ctrl+C stops both bun run --filter @thinkrail/cli dev # browser launcher bun run build:binary # standalone CLI artifact bun run desktop:dev # package and open the Electrobun app bun run desktop:build # package without opening it CONTRIBUTING.md covers the checks, the end-to-end suites, desktop packaging, and the repository layout. title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
body_text: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal - SimEdw's Blog simedw@blog $ cat ~/writing/world-model-terminal.md ~/writing ~/projects WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal 2026-10-21 / Simon Edwardsson / Follow @SimEdw / Discuss on HN ↗ TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell. The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly. When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs. Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal. A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print. What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output. The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos How it sees a terminal Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen. I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it. A session Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is. The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen. BOS SCREEN_START 32 96 ROW_0 0 'simedw@laptop:~$ ' CURSOR 0 17 1 SCREEN_END This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.) After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on. INPUT_START 'l' INPUT_END The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up: OUTPUT_START ROW_0 17 'l' CURSOR 0 18 1 OUTPUT_END In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it. Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones. I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two. Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own. Copying rows When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress. So I added a COPY operation instead: ROW_0 COPY 1 ROW_1 COPY 2 ROW_2 COPY 3 ... Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on. A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96. The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it. Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update. That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser. Generating the training data I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed. Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own. The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one. The synthetic recipe was: Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes. Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.). Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.). Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist. Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me. 35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state. The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size. I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training. Training I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage. I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal. Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves. In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session. Learning from its own mistakes To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations. 2 For each training example: Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output. Let the model predict the next 1-4 events. Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen. If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress. Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events. The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes. There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions. For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right. Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of. About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model. Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4. In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090. Testing I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data. The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training. 3 How much does fine-tuning help? Model 4 ShellBench /106 File readbacks /13 Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted 52 2 Qwen3-0.6B, prompted 60 3 WorldTUI 80 9 The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models. It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors , running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line. Making it fast For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal. But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen ( vim test.txt , man , clear ) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time. Rows in parallel What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update. That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps. The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates. This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s. Large-frame p95 latency (RTX 4090) ↓ Sequential 6.7 s Parallel rows 0.87 s Rows that can't talk to each other This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once. The solution was speculative decoding. Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass. Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially. The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft. In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like man test takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification. 5 Making it smaller I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, 6 so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB). I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB. The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab. Distilling Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output. My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens. That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory. In the end I gave up on distilling it. What it can do Memory This was the part I was most interested in. Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged. The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with cat , I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive! Other applications It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux. In vim, it handles the mode switch on esc and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode. Probably the most compute-intensive snake in the world. What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model. It even manages environment variables and variable expansion. Python Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: pythoon launches Python, but ython doesn't. What doesn't work I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring. Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations. Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path. There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency. In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause. Related work As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it. Back in 2022, people were already prompting ChatGPT to act as a Linux terminal . More recently, GameNGen simulated Doom using diffusion, and NeuralOS tackled a desktop GUI. WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux. Summary I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected. What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath. It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding. One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues. Try it here . It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find. I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here. It's monochrome: only characters, no colours or text styles. Unicode characters, including tmux's box-drawing borders, are mapped to ASCII before encoding, so those borders don't need multibyte character tokens.  ↩ Not too dissimilar to the scheduled sampling in my midi post .  ↩ These are short-gap tests, with 0–1 intervening commands. ShellBench also tests persistence across 18 commands.  ↩ Both prompted models got three worked examples each. They predict whole command outputs rather than individual screen updates, so it's not quite the same task.  ↩ Speculative decoding gives a much bigger speedup on a 4090 than on my M4. My suspicion is that the bottleneck shifts between compute and memory bandwidth, but I haven't investigated this properly.  ↩ Padded to 384 to please the GPUs.  ↩ Simon Edwardsson is co-founder of V7 , where he leads engineering and product.
