title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
body_text: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence Products Products Products Kimi Kimi Work Kimi Code Kimi Browser Extension Downloads All products Features Build AI app & website builder Slides AI presentation maker Docs AI document agent Sheets AI spreadsheet agent Deep Research AI research agent All features API API Use Cases Use Cases Featured use cases Build MVP sites Create portfolio sites Build blog sites Conduct academic research Conduct market research Create resumes Create brochures All use cases Featured tools AI landing page generator Image to website AI document generator PDF to PPT converter PDF translator AI Python code generator AI C++ code generator All capabilities Showcases Websites Agent Swarm Deep Research Slides Sheets Docs Design All showcases Business Business Kimi Business Business plans Contact sales Research Research Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3 PerceptionBench Kimi K2.6 Agent Swarm WorldVQA Kimi K2.5 Kimi Vendor Verifier Kimi K2 Thinking Kimi K2 All research Resources Resources Support & docs Help center Kimi Code docs Academy Kimi Work 101 Kimi Code 101 All tutorials Articles AI agents explained Multi-agent systems Parallel agents What is vibe coding Build a landing page Create a poster Write a business proposal All articles Pricing Pricing Download Download Download Download Try Kimi Scroll to explore Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities. We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions. Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4. Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% . Coding K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools. K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro: K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller. 3D Modeling and Design K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections. K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout. Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences: 3D Make is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere. Finance With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis. K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks: Financial Modeling evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points. Financial Research evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points. Business Operation evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance. Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's factual accuracy on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.) The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice: Cybersecurity As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness. Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example. Evaluation and results. After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits. On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance. Open-weight principles. These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure. Availability Kimi K3.1 Pro rolls out today across the Kimi product family: on Kimi.ai and the Kimi mobile apps, Kimi Work and Kimi Code, and through the Kimi API . Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026. Kimi Enterprise administrators can enable K3.1 Pro for their organization; access is off by default at launch. Details for each channel: Kimi Agents: Download or update to the latest Kimi app from your mobile app store, available on iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS, or visit kimi.ai . Work with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Download the latest Kimi Work desktop app , version 3.1.0 or later, available for Windows and Apple silicon Macs. Code with Kimi K3.1 Pro: Run Kimi Code and select Kimi K3.1 Pro using the /model command. Build with the Kimi API: Visit the Kimi API Platform and select kimi-k3.1-pro / kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed. Zero Data Retention is available for API customers. Bring Kimi to your organization: Kimi Business provides enterprise-grade data privacy and member management, with complete separation between personal and organization accounts. Visit the pricing page and select “Get Kimi Business” to subscribe for your team. Benchmarks Footnotes Unless otherwise specified, all Kimi K3.1 Pro results reported below are obtained with the reasoning effort set to 'max', temperature = 1.0, and top-p = 0.95. Coding benchmarks Terminal-Bench 4.0. Kimi K3.1 Pro is evaluated with the Claude-Code harness. The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is taken from the release blog ( https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ). All remaining scores are taken as the maximum value reported in either their blog posts or the official Terminal-Bench 4.0 leaderboard ( https://www.tbench.ai/ ). Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1. title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
body_text: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis | Lynch Lab Lynch Lab A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis I am a dermatologist. I tested the ability of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 to diagnosis skin cancer and found that they were less accurate than I expected. I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior. By Dr Magnus Lynch · 25 October 2026 · 5 min read This is a melanoma. Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view. It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer. The test # The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology: 100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses. 100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses. Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician. Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly. Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma. Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it. Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC. The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case. The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses. You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions. Correct first-choice diagnosis for the two LLMs and the CNN, which chose from the same six diagnoses. Labels show correct answers out of the number of lesions with that histology. The CNN was right more often overall and on most diagnoses. Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138. It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11. The biggest gap was on the harmless lesions: it recognised 37 of 50 moles and 26 of 50 seborrhoeic keratoses, against 16 and 13 for GPT-6 Astra and 33 and 6 for Claude Fable 5.1. It was one short of GPT-6 Astra on basal cell carcinoma and behind both LLMs on actinic keratosis. The models also failed differently. Each LLM had a favourite answer: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were. The CNN’s errors on melanoma went the other way: of the 17 it got wrong, it called 8 a naevus and 6 a seborrhoeic keratosis. The results in one table # GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 CNN (Inception v3) Correct diagnosis (of 200) 84 (42%) 85 (42%) 125 (62%) Correct in first or second choice 134 138 173 Melanoma as first choice (of 30) 8 11 13 Unsafe lesions kept (of 100) 97 96 77 at its preset threshold; 98 or 99 when matched Safe lesions discharged (of 100) 32 22 76 at its preset threshold Melanomas discharged (of 30) 3 4 18 at its preset threshold; 2 or 1 when matched Caveats # Small numbers. Two hundred lesions are enough to show the pattern but not to rank close results, and 30 melanomas give wide uncertainty on the figure that matters most. Each LLM case was run once; answers vary between runs. Hard cases. Every lesion was biopsied. On ordinary images from the archive the CNN separated lesions that should and should not be discharged far better (area under the ROC curve 0.96, against 0.86 here). Contamination. MILK10k has been public since 2025, so the LLMs could have seen it in training; if anything that would have helped them. The CNN certainly had not. Not state of the art. Inception v3 is a baseline. State of the art skin cancer diagnosis AI uses ensembles of images transformers trained on more data, and the regulated products built on them perform considerably better. Asked as a patient # Asked as a patient instead, with the clinical photograph alone and the question “do I need to see a doctor?”, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, harmless lesions included: for 99 and 98 of a further 100 biopsy-proven melanomas. Conclusion # A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs. Run it yourself # The cases, prompts, every LLM reply and the scoring code are in one download , and the CNN is here . I designed the test and made the clinical rulings. The analysis and the first drafts were produced with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which runs on a Claude model; one of the two LLMs tested is also Anthropic’s. Scoring was done by script against the histology. Images are from the MILK10k dataset (MILK study team, International Skin Imaging Collaboration), used under a CC BY-NC licence. Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London. His clinical work covers skin cancer, Mohs and facial reconstructive surgery, and lasers; his research covers the cell biology of skin cancers and scars and the use of AI in dermatology. Full profile .

title: Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models
body_text: How Cerebras Deploys Trillion-Parameter AI Models Skip to main content Products Customers Partners Developers Resources Pricing Company Contact us Get Started Oct 22 2026 How we deploy Trillion-parameter frontier models on Cerebras Sarah Chieng One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone. In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second. We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example. By the end, you'll understand: How we fit the full model into on-chip memory How we map the model across multiple chips How we handle a high # of concurrent requests Breaking it down with Kimi K3 Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers. It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here . For this illustrative example, we use: A 256k assumed average request size 4-bit weight quantization (like the Hugging Face implementation ) An 8-bit KV cache #1: Size of Each layer To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer. Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is: Dividing that payload by 93 layers then gives: #2: Number of Wafers Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type: Dense layers need additional room for a KV cache, because each dense (full-attention) layer stores the keys and values for every token in every active request. So, we place one dense layer per wafer and leave the remaining SRAM for its KV cache. Linear-attention layers do not require additional room for a KV cache. Instead of storing keys and values for every token, a linear-attention layer keeps a small, fixed-size state per request, regardless of context length. That leaves room for two linear layers per wafer (2 × 16 GB = 32 GB). Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers , we get: This gives us a total wafer count of 35 + 24 = 59 wafers. #3: Connecting the wafers together Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop. It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip. This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next. #4: How we serve 1 request Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages. For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token. #5: How we serve many requests This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one? No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time. While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them. Loading player... Each stage can also process a micro-batch , a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size. Loading player... To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput. #6: How many requests can we serve? The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers. For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with: Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case: Calculating the # of Concurrent Requests To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up: To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide: The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously. Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed. How this scales beyond 3T parameters The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip. Thanks for learning with us! title: Meta Employees Denounce Interference in Brazilian Elections
body_text: Meta Employees Denounce Interference in Brazilian Elections Subscribe Sign in News Meta Employees Denounce Interference in Brazilian Elections Meta staff are holding the Big Tech company’s leadership accountable for decisions they say could compromise the credibility of the democratic process. Panamerican Dispatch Oct 25, 2026 60 2 22 Share by ICL Noticias Employees at Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, have expressed concern over what they describe as “obvious” and “biased” favoritism toward members of the Bolsonaro family during Brazilian elections. In a statement, the company’s workers held Meta’s leadership responsible for decisions that, they argue, could undermine the credibility of the democratic process. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Subscribe Brazilians protest in front of the Meta building in London, UK, against the company’s interference in Brazil’s presidential elections. (Brasil Matters) The statement was signed by members of the tech sector branch of the United Kingdom’s Communication Workers Union , CWU. In the text, the employees voice concern regarding recent revelations about the company’s management and point to the risk of interference in the elections of other nations. “Since 2016, the political leanings of Meta executives and company leaders has been no secret,” the document states. The employees emphasize, however, that they consider this systematic and user-perceptible application of political favoritism to be unprecedented. “But this is the first time to our knowledge that favours made to politicians such as the Bolsonaros have been programmatically made user-facing to such an obvious and biased extent,” the statement reads. The text also expresses concern that the company’s actions could damage public trust in democratic institutions and in digital platforms themselves. “The last thing we want is to sit back and watch our employer interfering in the democratic processes of countries like Brazil,” the employees say. According to the group, a loss of credibility in elections and politicians could also erode trust in the technologies developed by the company. The employees warn that this scenario sets a dangerous precedent for the future. “We Meta employees want to build technologies and platforms that millions of people use and enjoy,” the text states. “In undermining the credibility of elections and politicians, it also unfairly undermines the credibility of what we build, and sets an incredibly dangerous precedent for the future. At the end of the statement, the employees call on the company to respect democratic principles. “We call for fairness and democracy to be respected,” the document concludes. On Saturday, October 24, a protest against Meta’s interventions in the Brazilian elections took place in front of the company’s headquarters in King’s Cross, central London. The demonstration was organized by the “Alliance for Democracy and Brazilian Sovereignty,” a collective of movements bringing together Brazilians in England. Brazilians protest in front of the Meta building in London, UK (Annaís Berlim/Brazil Matters) Below is the full text of the statement: As employees of Meta, we are disturbed by the revelations of the past few days and weeks regarding our management. Since 2016, the political leanings of Meta executives and company leaders has been no secret. But this is the first time to our knowledge that favours made to politicians such as the Bolsonaros have been programmatically made user-facing to such an obvious and biased extent. We Meta employees want to build technologies and platforms that millions of people use and enjoy. The last thing we want is to sit back and watch our employer interfering in the democratic processes of countries like Brazil. In undermining the credibility of elections and politicians, it also unfairly undermines the credibility of what we build, and sets an incredibly dangerous precedent for the future. We call for fairness and democracy to be respected. This article was originally published by ICL Noticias. It was translated by Panamerican Dispatch. title: The Goose Programming Language
body_text: The Goose Programming Language · Goose Goose Docs Tutorial Reference Spec Library Samples Benchmarks GitHub The Goose Programming Language Why Goose Features One memory model: data stacks freed at scope exit Memory never moves, so references survive growth Safe references, no annotations Nested data stays inline Enums in two sizes Links narrower than pointers Saving and loading data as bytes In-place construction Returning errors across calls Generics and function blocks Threads with no shared memory Compiling to and calling C Where the speed comes from Limitations Install a release Build and run Documentation Status License Authors History & Use of AI The Goose Programming Language A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory. Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Command line · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap . Every dynamic value lives inline on data stacks managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use. Why Goose Faster than C++ and than safe Rust, while memory safe. Over sixteen benchmarks Goose runs at 3.3x the speed of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++ and 1.12x the best safe Rust, and uses 1.9x, 1.3x and 1.2x less memory ( results ). These gains come from Goose's data layouts and memory model. No allocator, no GC, no reference counting, no destructors. Memory is a handful of data stacks that the compiler assigns statically. Freeing a structure with a million elements takes a single store, no matter how deeply it is nested. Growth preserves references. A reference into a growing array stays valid for as long as the array does. In the corresponding benchmarks, Goose keeps typed references where C++ must call reserve and safe Rust uses u32 indices. Memory safe with zero annotations. There is no lifetime syntax, there are no aliasing or exclusivity rules, and there is no unsafe . The compiler infers what every reference is rooted at and rejects references that could outlive their owners. Nested data stays inline. A string, an array of strings, a record with variable-size fields and an array of those records are each stored as one contiguous block that contains no pointers. A example record that takes 160 bytes and one allocation in C++ takes 29 bytes and no allocations in Goose. Variable sized Enums. Variable-mode ADTs store each value at the size of its own variant rather than that of the largest variant. On the benchmark that exercises this, they use 4x less memory than a Rust enum and run at 2x its speed. Links narrower than pointers. A relative reference stores a typed, checked link as a 1, 2 or 4-byte offset. Structures built from them are position independent, so a data structure can be written to a file as is. Saving it is a single write, and loading it is a single read followed by a verification pass that rejects malformed or hostile data. Everything is built in place, guaranteed. A value is constructed at its final destination through any depth of calls. items.push(parse(line)) writes the parsed record directly into the array, and returning a growable array by value does not copy it. Returns across multiple calls. return err from load returns from a function any number of frames up the call stack. It is checked statically, and needs no unwinder, no Result type and no ? on every call. Threads with no shared memory. A worker is compiled as a separate program with its own memory, and flat values are passed between threads through typed queues with a memcpy . Data races, locks, atomics and memory orderings do not exist in the language. Generics and higher-order functions with no overhead. An untyped parameter is generic. Function values are compile-time entities, so xs.filter() { it > 0 } compiles to what the handwrittend loop would looks like and builds its result directly in its destination. Compiles to C and can call C. Goose compiles to one C file, so it runs wherever a C compiler does and calls C directly through extern fn . The bundled TinyCC backend compiles and runs a program in-process, with no build step. The tutorial walks through all of this by example, the reference covers the whole language topic by topic, the specification has the exact rules, and the benchmarks have the numbers, including the cases where Goose loses. Features This section focuses on what distinguishes Goose. The tutorial explains these features in more detail, and the samples show them in thirty-one complete programs. One memory model: data stacks freed at scope exit A program has the native call stack, static data and N data stacks, where the compiler works out N. A data stack is a large address-space reservation with a bump pointer, and there is no other memory. At most one resizable value is live per stack and it is always on top, so growth never moves anything and never checks a capacity. All of this is proved at compile time; the runtime tracks only the bump pointers. for round in 3 { var scratch : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; // grow-only: growth is a pointer bump for i in 100000 { scratch . push ((i % 256 ) as ! u8 ) ; } print ( "round " , round , ": " , scratch . len , " bytes" ) ; } // the free: one store to the stack top Memory never moves, so references survive growth struct Item { id : i32 , weight : f32 } var items : Item [ >.. ] = [] ; let first .= items . push ( Item { 1 , 0.5 }) ; // a reference to element 0 for i : i32 in 2 .. 1000001 { items . push ( Item { i , 0.0 }) ; } first . weight = 99.5 ; // still valid, a million pushes later push returns a reference to the new element, so a program can link elements while building the array. A vector<T> or Vec<T> may reallocate and cannot provide this guarantee. Stable references account for several benchmark gains. Safe references, no annotations Every reference and slice has a static root : the variable that bounds its target's lifetime. A reference must not outlive the variable that owns its target or access that target through an incompatible type. The compiler infers roots and specializes functions for them, so no annotations are needed. There are no aliasing or exclusivity rules. When a lifetime check fails, the error names the reference's root and its destination: fn longest (a : u8 [ : ] , b : u8 [ : ]) -> u8 [ : ] { if a . len >= b . len { a } else { b } } var outer : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; var w = outer[ .. ] ; { var inner : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; format (inner , "inner text" ) ; w = longest (outer , inner) ; // error: storing a reference rooted at inner, } // which does not outlive the destination (§9.2) A slice T[:] lets a function accept a range from any array kind without copying its elements. For example, split returns slices into its input, and a dictionary keyed by u8[:] stores views of strings rather than copies. Nested data stays inline There is no single array type. Instead there is a family of array types that differ only in how their size can change. Every member is laid out as [metadata][elements...] , inline and packed, never as a pointer to a separate block of elements: Type What it is T[k] fixed size, known at compile time T[] , T[varint] sized at construction, frozen after; a fixed or variable-width length T[..k] , T[..] capacity inline; grows and shrinks within it T[>..] grow-only : the most commonly used kind; references into it stay valid T[>..<] grow-shrink : stacks, queues, heaps Strings are u8 arrays: u8[>..] is a builder, u8[] a finished string stored inline in whatever holds it, u8[..16] a small string inside a struct, u8[:] a view. A struct may contain variable-size parts, which are stored inline in declaration order, so a record is a sequence of bytes with no indirection in it: struct Item { sku : u8 [ varint ] , qty : varint , cents : varint } struct Order { id : varint , customer : u8 [ varint ] , items : Item [ varint ] } var book : Order [ >.. ] = [] ; book . push ( Order { id : 1001 , customer : "alice" , items : [ Item { sku : "SKU-441" , qty : 2 , cents : 1999 } , Item { sku : "SKU-7" , qty : 1 , cents : 500 }] }) ; That order is 29 bytes and 0 allocations . As C++ std::string + std::vector<Item> it is 160 bytes and 1 allocation, and as Rust String + Vec<Item> it is 153 bytes and 4 allocations. An entire order book is a single array, so reading it streams through the cache. The trade-off is that an array of variable-size elements is sequential: you can iterate it but not index it (unless you keep a second array of references into it as an index). Enums in two sizes Algebraic data types are the only form of dynamic polymorphism; there is no inheritance and there are no vtables. Every ADT can be stored in two ways, chosen at the point of use. Fixed mode ( Shape ) stores a tag plus room for the largest payload, so values can be indexed and overwritten. Variable mode ( Shape.. ) gives each value exactly the size of its variant. An array of such values becomes sequential and a value never changes variant, but in exchange you may take references into a payload: enum Shape { Circle { r : f64 } , Rect { w : f64 , h : f64 } , Dot } var packed : Shape .. [ >.. ] = [] ; // 9, 17 and 1 bytes, not 17 each packed . push ( Shape . Circle { r : 1.0 }) ; packed . push ( Shape . Rect { w : 2.0 , h : 3.0 }) ; packed . push ( Shape . Dot ) ; for s in packed { match s { Rect & r => { r . w += 1.0 ; } , _ => {} } // edits the payload in place, inside the array } Case functions provide another way to dispatch on a variant: define one overload per variant. Calls dispatch on the tag through a jump table, and the compiler checks that the overloads cover every variant: fn area (s : Shape . Circle ) -> f64 { 3.14159 * s . r * s . r } fn area (s : Shape . Rect ) -> f64 { s . w * s . h } fn area (s : Shape . Dot ) -> f64 { 0.0 } for s in packed { print (s , " area " , area (s)) ; } Links narrower than pointers A T& is a machine address: it takes eight bytes and never dangles. A relative reference is the same link stored as a narrow offset. A T&<u32> is measured from the field itself to a target in the same array, so the structure is position independent. A T&<u32 in pool> is measured from the base of a named pool, so other arrays can link into the pool. T&<u32>? uses offset 0 as null. Here is a binary search tree in one grow-only array, with 12-byte nodes: struct Node { key : i32 , left : Node &< u32 >?, right : Node &< u32 >? } // 12 bytes, links included fn insert (pool : Node [ >.. ] &, key : i32 ) { if pool . len == 0 { pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; return ; } var cur .= pool[ 0 ] ; // .= binds a reference; = would copy the node loop { if key == cur . key { return ; } let next = if key < cur . key { cur . left } else { cur . right } ; if next { cur .= next ; continue ; } // narrowed by `if`: next is a Node& if key < cur . key { cur . left .= pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; } else { cur . right .= pool . push ( Node { key : key }) ; } return ; } } References are transparent (there is no * or -> ). .= binds or retargets a reference, and Node? is a nullable reference that if , guard and assert narrow. The insert is one push and one store, and the push cannot invalidate cur . When lifetimes are not nested, a reusable pool pairs a grow-only array with a hidden freelist. alloc_ref reuses a free slot or pushes a new one, and free returns a slot to the pool. Since a slot's memory is never actually freed, a stale slot reads a different value of the correct type rather than corrupting memory. Saving and loading data as bytes var image : u8 [ >.. ] = tree . to_bytes () ; // a framed byte image of the whole array var loaded , ok = from_bytes < Node [ >.. ] > (image) ; // verified before it becomes a value image[image . len - 3 ] = 200 ; // tamper with a link ... var bad , bok = from_bytes < Node [ >.. ] > (image) ; // ... and it is false and an empty array The tree's links are self-relative, so the tree means the same thing wherever it is stored. Saving it writes its bytes and loading it reads them back, with no serializer, no schema and no pointer fixups. from_bytes checks the framing, every tag, every length and every link before the bytes become a value, so a corrupt or hostile file makes it return false , never a wild reference. In-place construction The copy-free construction guarantee ( spec §4.3 ) says a constructed value is always built at its final location, which is passed down through calls. A function returning a grow-only array by value writes its elements directly into the caller's variable, or into a field of the record being built inside another array, so out-parameters are rarely needed. words . push ( str ( "word" , i)) ; // formatted straight into the new element let evens = xs . filter () { it % 2 == 0 } ; // built straight into `evens`: no temporary book . push ( Order { id : 1001 , customer : "alice" , items : parse_items ( "SKU-441:2:1999;SKU-7:1:500" ) }) ; Returning errors across calls struct User { name : u8 [ .. 16 ] , age : i32 } fn load (text : u8 [ : ]) -> User [ >.. ] , u8 [] { var users : User [ >.. ] = [] ; each_split (text , ' \n ' ) { users . push ( parse_user (it)) ; } ; return users , "" ; } fn parse_user (line : u8 [ : ]) -> User { // returns a User: no Result, no error parameter let comma = find (line , "," ) ; guard comma >= 0 else { return [] , str ( "expected name,age: " , line) from load ; } let age , ok = parse_int (line[comma + 1 .. ]) ; guard ok else { return [] , str ( "bad age: " , line) from load ; } let name = trim (line[ .. comma]) ; return User { name : name , age : age as i32 } ; } return E from f returns E as the result of the innermost active call of f , however many frames up that call is. Every function in between keeps its plain signature. The construct is checked statically: every call of parse_user must lie inside a load call, so nothing can go uncaught at runtime. It is implemented as a hidden discriminant checked in each frame rather than as an unwinder, and the message is built directly where load 's caller wants it. The parsers in the samples use it for every syntax error. Generics and function blocks fn twice (x) { x + x } // an untyped parameter is a generic one fn each_pair < T , F > (xs : T [ : ]) { // F is a function value: a compile-time entity for i in 0 .. xs . len - 1 { F (xs[i] , xs[i + 1 ]) ; } } fn first_gap (xs : i64 [ : ]) -> i64 { each_pair (xs) { a , b => if b - a > 1 { return a ; } } ; // returns from first_gap, not each_pair return - 1 ; } let evens = xs . filter () { it % 2 == 0 } ; let total = fold (xs , 0 ) { acc , x => acc + x } ; sort (xs) { a , b => a > b } ; Everything is monomorphized. Type arguments are inferred from argument types; type parameters that do not appear in those types can be supplied explicitly. Function values are passed as generic parameters. Every call of a function value is direct and can be inlined, function values cannot escape, and there are no closure objects or function pointers, so a higher-order function compiles to exactly the loop it looks like. A block may return from its lexically enclosing function, and nested functions can use the enclosing function's locals. Threads with no shared memory thread_fn worker () { // a separate program with its own memory loop { let job = qget < Job > () ; // blocks on the typed queue for Job guard job . n >= 0 else { break ; } // -1 means stop qput ( Result { n : job . n , digits : count_digits (job . n) }) ; } } for i in n { ids . push ( thread_spawn (worker)) ; } There is no shared mutable memory. A thread_fn and everything it calls is compiled as its own program with its own data stacks and its own copies of the globals. Values are passed between threads through typed queues, one per type, and must be flat , with no references at any depth. Passing them is cheap because a flat Goose value is contiguous: a job or a result can carry real data, such as pixels, and passing it is a single memcpy . A failed check or abort in a worker started with thread_spawn_contained ends only that worker. Its message goes to whoever waits for it, not to stderr, so a supervisor can log it and start another: var why : u8 [ >.. ] = [] ; while ! thread_wait ( thread_spawn_contained (serve , attempt) , why) { log (why) ; // "assert failed (serve.goose:12)" why . clear () ; attempt ++; } The first thread_wait(id, msg) for a worker takes the message; a caller that doesn't ask for it loses it. Compiling to and calling C extern fn hypot (x : f64 , y : f64 ) -> f64 ; // straight from libm extern fn crc32_bytes (s : const u8 [ : ]) -> u32 ; // a slice crosses as { data, len } extern fn stats_of (xs : i32 [ : ] , out : Stats & ) ; // a struct filled through a pointer An extern fn binds a Goose signature to a C symbol. The math and os modules use this interface. Only types with supported C representations may cross the boundary; unsupported signatures are rejected at the declaration. The compiler emits one C file for the whole program. The bundled TinyCC backend can compile and run that C inside the Goose compiler's process. Where the speed comes from Much of the speed comes from the memory model: no heap allocation or per-object teardown, contiguous data, narrow links, and enums sized for the variant they contain. Every index is bounds-checked, and the compiler removes checks it can prove unnecessary. An assert on a slice length often lets the compiler remove the remaining checks in a kernel, so that the kernel can be vectorized. --bce-lines reports the checks that remain. checkfree fn rejects a kernel if any bounds check remains in it; index types let graph edges keep the validation done while the graph was built. Benchmark measurements use whole-process wall-clock time, including teardown. Geometric mean over 16 benchmarks vs idiomatic C++ vs hand-optimized C++ vs best safe Rust speed, MSVC backend 3.51x 1.24x 1.13x speed, clang backend 3.54x 1.26x 1.19x peak memory 1.95x less 1.32x less 1.25x less The summary explains the gains and losses; results.md has every measurement, and design.md explains what the suite tests. Limitations You have to think about where data lives: who owns it, and how long its scope lasts. Usually the owner is the function that builds the data, which needs no extra work; when it is not, the data goes in a reusable pool. Recursive functions cannot keep growable data across a recursive call. Scratch data must end before the call, and data that outlives the call is passed in as a pool. Arrays of variable-size elements can be iterated but not indexed (unless you keep an index of references beside them). A fixed-mode enum cannot be pointed into, and a variable-mode one cannot be overwritten. You make this choice per container. There are no escaping closures, no function pointers and no dynamic dispatch beyond ADT tags, and only whole-program compilation is supported. A slot that was returned to a reusable pool but is still referenced reads whatever its next owner put there. That is a logic bug, but never memory corruption. Tutorial §18 is the full list. Install a release Prebuilt compilers for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) are on the releases page , with the graphics, audio, ui and physics packages compiled in. Unpack one anywhere and put its directory on PATH: the compiler finds the standard library, TinyCC's runtime and the packages beside itself, and keeps what it builds under ~/.goose ( GOOSE_HOME ). The archive also holds these docs, the samples and the VS Code extension. Running a program in-process ( goose file.goose ) needs nothing else on Windows. On Linux it needs the C library's headers ( libc6-dev , or glibc-devel ); on macOS, the SDK of the Xcode command line tools ( xcode-select --install ). goose build also needs a C compiler: Visual Studio 2022 or later, or clang, on Windows; gcc or clang elsewhere. The Linux compiler needs glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12), and the macOS compiler needs macOS 13.3 or later. macOS keeps a downloaded archive's files from running until xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine is run on the unpacked directory. Build and run You need CMake 3.27 or later, a C++20 compiler (MSVC, clang or gcc) and Python 3 for the test and sample runners. TinyCC, which the in-process backend is built from, is part of the tree. The graphics, audio, ui and physics modules are packages in repositories of their own ( goose_gfx and goose_physics ; docs/design/packages.md ). -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all fetches them with git at configure time, at the pinned tags, and compiles them into the compiler, so programs that use them run with nothing else installed. Without that option the compiler is built on its own, and the first time a program imports one of these packages, the package is built into ~/.goose , which needs git, cmake and a C compiler. git clone https://github.com/aardappel/goose cd goose cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE = Release -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS = all cmake --build build --config Release GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS can also name some of the packages ( physics , or gfx , which includes audio and ui too). On Linux, SDL needs the X11 or Wayland development packages ( third_party/SDL/docs/README-linux.md ); without them the build leaves the gfx module out and says what to install. The runner scripts prefer build/Release , then build/RelWithDebInfo , then build , then build/Debug . Pass --exe to select a specific compiler; use an explicit Debug executable when testing with compiler assertions enabled. The compiler is build/goose ( build/Release/goose.exe with the Visual Studio generator), and it finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from. On Windows 10 version 1903 and later, its embedded manifest selects a UTF-8 process code page so compiler paths do not depend on the system locale. Earlier Windows versions retain their legacy code page. Generated native executables retain their own process settings. Run a program directly from source, in-process, with no C compiler and no build step ( goose run is the explicit form of the same command): build/goose samples/01_tour.goose Or build an executable, which is written beside the source. The compiler finds a C compiler on the machine ( goose toolchain shows which one) and links the generated C with the runtime and any native modules the program uses, including graphics. Programs that use threads must be built this way, since TinyCC cannot place thread-local storage. build/goose build samples/01_tour.goose && samples/01_tour build/goose build samples/27_gfx_cube.goose && samples/27_gfx_cube goose check only typechecks. --debug turns on the overflow, range and tag checks, each of which names its source line when it fails, and --bce-lines reports the bounds checks that remain on each line. Every resizable value lives on a data stack of 2 GB of reserved address space, committed as it is used, and --stack-reserve 16G changes that size. The command line describes every command and option, including how to write the C for a build system or a C host of your own ( goose -o tour.c tour.goose ). A program with C of its own lists that C in a sidecar file beside the source, foo.build beside foo.goose : c_sources = ["impl.c"]; . Both forms build that C, so an extern fn can call it either way. A program uses a library by writing import name from "source"; in its root file. The source is a directory ( "./lib" ), or a git repository at a tag or commit ( "owner/repo@v1" on GitHub, "host/owner/repo@ref" ), which is fetched into ~/.goose and built there once per C compiler ( packages ). A program using audio plays procedural mono/stereo PCM through SDL3 without opening a graphics window. See the audio reference . The test suite and the samples run on Windows, macOS and Linux: python test/run_tests.py python samples/run_samples.py For editing, the VS Code extension gives syntax highlighting, the compiler's language server ( goose lsp : errors as you type, hover, go to definition, completion, rename, symbols) and one-key runs through the JIT: code --install-extension vscode/goose-language.vsix Other editors can run goose lsp themselves; editors has the configuration for Neovim, Helix and Emacs. Documentation Documentation index : the map of everything below, and the root of the documentation site built from these files ( how ). Tutorial : the friendly introduction, by example. Read this first. Language reference : every feature, topic by topic, with a compiling example for each. It covers the whole language and is written to be read. Language specification : the exact rules, when you want to know why something did not compile. Samples : thirty-one complete programs in reading order, from a tour of the language to a JSON parser, a threaded Mandelbrot, a file tree built from two pools, a spinning cube on the GPU, thousands of boxes raining into a heap and a to-do list in windows of widgets. Standard library : fourteen modules, all written in readable Goose under stdlib/ . They include gfx for graphics on SDL3's GPU API ( how it is built ) and physics for rigid body physics on Box3D ( how it is built ). The ui module provides fonts, text rendering and game HUDs . It also provides windows and widgets on Nuklear, drawn through gfx ( how it is built ). The command line : every command and option of goose , from running and building to writing the C yourself, the formatter and the language server. Building programs and using packages : libraries from git repositories or directories, a program's own C, and how to make a package of your own. Benchmarks : the numbers, with the full results and the design behind them. Implementation notes : how the compiler works, pass by pass, and how it is tested . Status Goose is new. What exists today is a whole-program compiler of about thirty thousand lines of C++, the specification, the standard library, the samples, and a test suite that CI runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with an extra sanitizer job. These are deliberately out of scope for now: moves for resizable values, more than one resizable per struct, labeled break , namespace privacy, and more OS/library access. Open items are tracked in the specification's Appendix B . License Goose is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 . Authors Wouter van Oortmerssen : Language Design, Compiler Design, Coding standards. home page, twitter . Claude Fable : Compiler implementation, Benchmarking, Sample & Doc writing. History & Use of AI This repo was produced almost entirely with AI, from a human language design. I had designed Goose several years ago, and had started to implement it, but running a game startup (which is built on another programming language of mine, Lobster ) there was no time to finish it. Which was sad, because I knew Goose could do things other languages can't, and it should exist. I had not expected AI to help with this until Fable came out. I thought it might be capable enough to do a good job. I made it essentially clone the style and structure of my other recent compiler (Lobster), which is why if you look at the code, it looks rather similar to that. My initial design had left lots of things unspecified, and lots of back and forth with Fable made me decide on all of those, and it is now a better language for it. It is also an experiment in using AI to implement a new language, rather than reproduce an existing one. You may wonder why I had it work in C++, if clearly I could have used any language, like Rust, or my own Lobster, or.. Goose itself (that may still happen). With Fable, it was my observation that it is almost equally capable in any language, and the strong guardrails of Rust or other languages are not as pressing as they once were. Since the compiler emits C, you likely already need to have a C/C++ compiler around, so sticking inside one ecosystem would seem to simplify deployment and adoption. I've also integrated libtcc and who knows what other C libraries in the future. And, like I said, to have the compiler code mimic my existing Lobster compiler seemed fun, at least I can read it like it is my own. Built from README.md .

"/> AI use leads UC Berkeley math professor to see ‘no point’ in grading homework Audrey Baime | Staff Audrey Baime Oct 23, 2026 Oct 23, 2026 Comments Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Prolific student AI use and advancements in AI technology leaves the future of mathematics uncertain. Isaac Kim | Staff Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Richard Borcherds, a UC Berkeley professor and Fields medalist, no longer grades his students’ homework. After seeing how many of his students used AI to consistently receive top scores, he felt there was “no point” in paying readers to grade for correctness in homework, as AI use is now unavoidable. Borcherds revealed this in a sit-down interview Tuesday, following OpenAI’s announcement that AI agents apparently solved one of mathematics’ most difficult unsolved problems, the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem. “If AI continues to improve at present rate, then, in a few years, there’ll be nothing human mathematicians can do that AI can’t do better,” Borcherds said. Borcherds said he currently grades on completion if a student hands in their homework. He admitted that it is “not a very good system,” but at the moment, he has no alternative. Borcherds stated he no longer knows whether to encourage students to go into the math department , as it seemed five years ago that being a mathematician was one of the safest careers from the AI boom. “I have no idea what to advise. I even asked ChatGPT this exact question, and even ChatGPT said it didn’t have any idea what was going to happen,” Borcherds said. He described a plentiful amount of “inertia” in the academic system and said he wouldn’t be surprised if things stayed the same in the math department for a couple years despite AI developments. He drew a comparison to physical paper journals, which publish even though they have been “utterly pointless” for two decades. “There have been plenty of technical breakthroughs in the past — hand weaving was put out of business by looms, and horses were put out of business by motor cars, and so on,” Borcherds said. “This is the first time anything like this has happened in mathematics, though.” The Berkeley Division of the Academic Senate asks that faculty include a statement about course expectations including the use of AI tools for coursework in course syllabi, according to an email from Anne Marie Richard, assistant vice provost for undergraduate education and chief academic technology officer. However, she said the direct policies on AI use can vary dramatically with course level and focus area . Campus has tried several AI detection tools, including Turnitin and Rumi , but have determined that these tools aren’t adequate enough to be standardized on campus. AI policy for classes is up to the discretion of faculty, but there is a growing database of sample AI use statements available in the AI Hub, the campus directory for AI tools, training and policies, for faculty to use in their syllabi, according to Richard. title: Broccoli2Shell: Brotli decoder RCE in Node.js, Python and more
body_text: Broccoli2Shell: Brotli decoder RCE (CVE-2026-111497) in Node.js, Python and more CVE-2026-111497 Broccoli 2Shell A bug in the Brotli decoder lets crafted compressed data write past the end of a buffer. Node.js, Python and anything else built on Google's C decoder needs a patch. See affected versions How to fix it 9.2 Critical CVE-2026-111497 Recall notice Brotli decoder 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. An out-of-bounds write that can lead to a crash, a memory leak or remote code execution. Rated 9.2 Critical (CVSS 4.0) by GitHub, High by Node.js. Affected versions and their replacements Product Affected Fixed in Google Brotli (C library) 1.0.3 â 1.2.0 1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1 Node.js 26 below 26.12.1 26.12.1 Node.js 24 below 24.22.1 24.22.1 Node.js 22 below 22.23.4 22.23.4 Node.js 25, 23, 20 and older all versions No fix. These lines are end of life, so move to 22, 24 or 26. Python Brotli 1.0.3 â 1.2.0 1.2.1 Python brotlicffi 1.0.3 â 1.2.0.x 1.2.1.0 Installing the update isn't enough. A running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts, and a container keeps it until you rebuild the image on a patched base and redeploy. Who's exposed The bug Python Other software Bundled copies Check Fix Exploitation Timeline Why broccoli Sources Who's exposed You're at risk if your code, or any library it uses, decompresses Brotli data that someone else controls. That happens in more places than you'd think, because HTTP clients decompress Brotli responses on their own. Your app fetches a URL Node's built-in fetch() decodes Content-Encoding: br responses automatically. So do Python's requests / urllib3 and aiohttp whenever a Brotli package is installed. Any server you talk to can send the payload, whether through webhooks, link previews, crawlers or "import from URL" features. Your app accepts uploads or request bodies Express 5.0.0â5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0â2.3.0 inflate Brotli request bodies in parsers such as raw() and json() . Python frameworks and middleware that decode br bodies are exposed in the same way. A bare node:http server doesn't decode bodies by itself. Your app calls the decoder directly This means zlib.brotliDecompress*() , createBrotliDecompress() , brotli.decompress() , and any library that uses them on archives, caches or queue messages. Express and body-parser don't contain the bug. They're just paths to it, so upgrading them won't help. Node.js bundles its own copy of Brotli, which means the system libbrotli doesn't matter there. Only the Node.js version does. The bug A Brotli stream is split into blocks, and the decoder switches between block types as it reads them. Before the fix, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() in c/dec/decode.c returned a plain boolean, so callers couldn't tell a malformed stream from one that just needed more input. On the fast path, the decoder ignored the return value altogether. A crafted stream can request a block switch that can't happen. The decoder took that to mean "need more input" and kept adding attacker bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, writing past its end. The overwrite corrupts nearby decoder state. That's how a malformed stream can turn into a memory leak or code execution. The upstream fix is google/brotli commit 0ed4268 , along with 50a9b70 , b418fa8 and da98063 . It returns a hard format error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (â17), to the caller. The bug is tracked as CWE-252 (unchecked return value) and CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). Python The PyPI packages Brotli and brotlicffi compile the same C decoder. Your code doesn't need to import them to be exposed. If either one is installed, these clients use it on their own: urllib3 , and therefore requests , advertises Accept-Encoding: br and decodes Brotli responses. aiohttp uses Brotli when it's installed. httpx uses it through the httpx[brotli] extra. Scrapy and other crawlers. Some versions install Brotli as a dependency. Don't wait for your scanner. When this was disclosed, pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety didn't reliably flag the affected PyPI versions. The CVE record named the upstream Google repository, not the PyPI packages. GitHub's advisory now lists both packages (PYSEC-2026-4322 and PYSEC-2026-4323), but check by hand anyway. If your bindings come from your Linux distribution (for example python3-brotli ) and not from PyPI, the fix arrives through your distribution's security updates. Other software The bug is in Google's reference C decoder, not in Node.js or Python. Anything that ships or links Brotli 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 may be affected, even before an advisory names it. The system library. It's called libbrotlidec , packaged as libbrotli1 , brotli and similar. Programs that link it dynamically are fixed once your distribution ships a patched package and you restart them. Statically linked or vendored copies need their own rebuild. Bindings that wrap the C code. This covers Java JNI wrappers, PHP and Ruby extensions, and Go cgo bindings. Look for a release that bundles 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1. Proxies, CDNs, HTTP clients and archive tools that decode br content with the C library. Decoders rewritten in other languages aren't a concern. The Java, JavaScript and C# ports, which pdf.js, iText and HtmlUnit use, can't reach the bug. The Go port (andybalholm/brotli) had the same logic error, but it would only have crashed, and it was fixed on 23 October. Rust's brotli-decompressor catches the condition and returns an error. Code execution is only possible in the C decoder. Projects that bundle their own copy Many projects ship a private copy of the C decoder instead of using your system's library. A distribution update doesn't fix those: each project has to update its copy. We searched GitHub for vendored copies and read their headers, and last rechecked them on 25 October 2026. A copy is patched if it includes the new BLOCK_SWITCH error code. Not fixed yet, as of 26 October Project Bundled copy Untrusted input it decodes DuckDB unpatched Brotli-compressed Parquet files. A fix is in progress in PR #27791 . Apache Arrow (bundled build) 1.0.9 Brotli-compressed Parquet files. Tracked in issue #55166 . PR #55167 , which moves to Brotli 1.0.10, has been approved but not merged. v8-jsi 1.2.0 The same paths as Node.js, because it bundles Node.js 7-Zip-zstd 1.2.0 Archives and .br files a user opens. Tracked in issue #579 . p7zip 1.0.9 Archives and .br files a user opens EDK II 1.2.0 Compressed firmware sections. Tracked in issue #13378 . woff2 (Makefile build) 1.0.3 WOFF2 fonts passed to woff2_decompress . The CMake build links the system library instead. Tracked in issue #207 . A fix has been proposed in PR #208 . Fixed since disclosure Project Fixed in Details Ruby brotli gem 0.9.1 Bundles Brotli 1.2.1 and refuses to build against an unpatched system libbrotli. Released on 24 October ( issue #64 ). .NET runtime 8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14 Also 11.0.0-rc.3. Covers BrotliStream , BrotliDecoder , HttpClient automatic decompression and ASP.NET Core request decompression . Released on 25 October ( advisory ). The public GitHub branches have not caught up with the internal fix yet, so source builds from GitHub are still affected. PHP brotli extension 0.21.1 Bundles Brotli 1.2.1. Released on 24 October ( PR #105 ). UEFITool A76 Bundles Brotli 1.2.1. Released on 24 October ( issue #492 ). MuPDF 1.28.0 Its Brotli fork picked up the upstream fix in April 2026, before disclosure, so every 1.28.x release is patched. The 1.27.x releases still bundle the affected decoder. ClickHouse master branch Updated to Brotli 1.2.1 in PR #127419 on 25 October and backported to 26.10. Backports to 26.9, 26.8 and 26.3 LTS are open. Not in a release yet: the latest, 26.10.2.103, came out before the fix. NanaZip main branch Updated to Brotli 1.2.1 in 3da1c6a on 24 October. Not in a release yet: the latest, 7.0.1873.0, came out before the fix. GraalJS (graal-nodejs) master branch The fix was merged on 22 October. Not in a release yet: GraalVM ships security updates quarterly, and the latest release, 25.4.4.1.1, came out before the fix. YDB main branch Patched with the upstream fix in 343f6be on 23 October. Not in a release yet. libjxl main branch Updated to Brotli 1.2.1 in PR #5062 on 24 October. Not in a release yet: the latest, v0.12.0, came out before the fix. Fixed before this list was made: Node.js, Bun, Chromium, Firefox, brotlicffi, ngx_brotli, Brotli4j, SumatraPDF, Ghostscript, CatBoost and YTsaurus, as well as Gentoo, Solus and VMware Photon packages. This list isn't complete. GitHub's code search skips submodules and some very large repositories, and private or vendored-at-build-time copies don't show up at all. A project listed here may not reach the decoder in every configuration. If you maintain one of these projects, updating to 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (or cherry-picking commit 0ed4268 ) fixes it. Check your versions Node.js node --version # affected if below 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1, or on an end-of-life line # the Brotli version bundled into this Node binary node -p "process.versions.brotli" # inside a container image docker run --rm --entrypoint node <image> --version Python pip show Brotli brotlicffi # what pulls it in pipdeptree -r -p Brotli # lockfiles grep -i brotli poetry.lock uv.lock requirements*.txt Pipfile.lock 2>/dev/null # inside a container image docker run --rm --entrypoint pip <image> show Brotli brotlicffi System library dpkg -l | grep -i brotli # Debian, Ubuntu rpm -qa | grep -i brotli # RHEL, Fedora apk info -v | grep -i brotli # Alpine # running processes that have the decoder loaded sudo grep -l brotlidec /proc/*/maps 2>/dev/null Check everywhere code runs: production, staging, CI runners, build images, serverless runtimes and developer laptops. Patch first any service that fetches URLs you don't control or accepts Content-Encoding: br bodies. Fix it Upgrade # Node.js: through your version manager, base image or package source nvm install 24.22.1 # or 22.23.4 / 26.12.1 FROM node:24.22.1-slim # Dockerfile # Python pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0" # then raise the constraint and regenerate poetry.lock / uv.lock / requirements.txt Then restart every process, rebuild every image and redeploy. Update the pins in your lockfiles, or the next build will reinstall the vulnerable version. If you can't upgrade yet Python: uninstall Brotli and brotlicffi . urllib3, requests and aiohttp will fall back to gzip and deflate. Remove extras such as httpx[brotli] too, or the next install brings the package back. Inbound: reject Content-Encoding: br request bodies at your proxy, load balancer or WAF. Several providers, including Vercel, deployed WAF rules for this on disclosure day. Outbound: removing br from Accept-Encoding helps less than you'd hope, because a malicious server can send Brotli anyway. A WAF doesn't see responses your app fetches. Only the runtime or library upgrade covers that path. Node.js has published no workaround. For Node.js, upgrading the runtime is the only complete fix. Exploitation status Imperva Red Team ran attacker-supplied code on the official, unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image. They delivered the payload both as a fetched response and as an Express request body. It took several attempts, and they haven't released the exploit. A public proof of concept appeared on GitHub on 2026-10-22. It reportedly reaches code execution only on a deliberately weakened build. On standard builds it causes a crash and a limited memory read. For Python , researchers confirmed the bug with AddressSanitizer. Version 1.2.0 accepted a crafted stream of about 23 MB, and 1.2.1 rejected it with error â17. They didn't attempt an exploit. As of 2026-10-22, no attacks in the wild had been reported. With public PoCs out, expect that to change. Timeline Feb 2026 The fix first lands in the Brotli source, per OpenSourceMalware's analysis. 21 Oct 2026 Node.js releases 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1. Google releases Brotli 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1. 22 Oct 2026 NVD publishes CVE-2026-111497 and GitHub publishes GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35. Brotli 1.2.1 reaches PyPI, Imperva publishes its research, and a public PoC appears. 23 Oct 2026 brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 reaches PyPI. Researchers publish the Python impact analysis, and GitHub adds the PyPI packages to its advisory. Why broccoli Lately every serious bug comes with a something 2shell domain, and people race to register them. Some of those sites have ended up taking credit for work done by other people. This bug was first called "Node2Shell", but the flaw is in Brotli itself and reaches well beyond Node.js. Juliano Rizzo had a better idea : âThe Brotli bug (think zlib 20 years ago) is a bigger deal than PHP2Shell [â¦] Node2Shell is a terrible name. I'm calling it Broccoli.â Juliano Rizzo, @julianor To be clear: we didn't find this bug. We just registered a domain named after a vegetable. Credit goes to the people who did the work. OpenAI Codex Security (Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer) reported it to Node.js. Matteo Collina and Antoine du Hamel fixed it in Node.js. The Imperva Red Team (Ron Masas) did the exploitation research. OpenSourceMalware and Aikido analyzed the Python impact. Sources Node.js: October 2026 security releases GitHub Advisory GHSA-9v8h-qqgm-4m35 NVD: CVE-2026-111497 CVE.org record google/brotli releases 1.0.10, 1.1.1 and 1.2.1 Imperva: From Brotli data to remote code execution OpenSourceMalware: Python packages are affected too Aikido: Python packages are also vulnerable Vercel: Node.js security advisory Last updated 26 October 2026. This page is independent and not affiliated with Google, the Node.js project or the Python Software Foundation. When in doubt, the vendor advisories above are authoritative. Set in Archivo .
